notes.en: The first major section of Leviticus deals with the institution of the sacrificial system and the priesthood. The sacrifices were either for atonement (the whole burnt offering, sin offering, and guilt offering) or for worship (grain offering and peace offering). Each one taught theology through a hands-on approach. Priests were required to officiate in the sacrificial worship at the Tabernacle, to instruct God’s people in the revelation given to Moses at Sinai, and to represent the people before God, such as on the Day of Atonement (ch 16). Priests were provided for by receiving a portion of the offerings.

notes.title: 1:1–7:38 總覽
notes.zh: 利未記的第一大段論到獻祭制度和祭司職分的設立。這些祭有的是為了贖罪（燔祭、贖罪祭、贖愆祭），有的是為了敬拜（素祭、平安祭）。每一種祭都用親手實行的方式教導屬靈的真理。祭司要在會幕主持獻祭的敬拜，把神在西奈山向摩西啟示的話教導百姓，並在神面前代表百姓，例如在贖罪日（第16章）。祭司的生活所需，靠從各種供物中分得的一份來供應。

notes.en: The Lord called to Moses from the Tabernacle: Leviticus is part of the ongoing narrative of the Pentateuch (Gen 1:1—Deut 34:12). It is part of the history of God’s saving acts: God chose Israel to be his people, delivered them from slavery in Egypt, entered into a covenant relationship with them, and guided them through the desert to the Promised Land. Specifically, Leviticus picks up with events recorded in Exod 40:34-38, when construction of the Tabernacle is completed. It has been dedicated, and the Lord has filled it with his glory. Now the Lord gives Moses instructions for conducting worship at the Tabernacle. • The Tabernacle (literally Tent of Meeting; see study note on Exod 27:21) was an earthly representation of God’s palace. Inside the Most Holy Place, the Ark of the Covenant represented God’s throne (Exod 40:1-33). The Lord’s glory resided between the outstretched wings of the cherubim. There he would meet with Israel to communicate his will to them (see Exod 25:22).

excerpts.zh: 耶和華從會幕中呼叫摩西

notes.zh:
「耶和華從會幕中呼叫摩西」：利未記是摩西五經（創1:1—申34:12）連貫敘事的一部分，也是神拯救作為的歷史的一部分：神揀選以色列作祂的子民，救他們脫離在埃及為奴之地，與他們立約，又帶領他們走過曠野，前往應許之地。具體來說，利未記接續出埃及記40:34-38的事件：會幕已經造好、獻上，耶和華的榮光也充滿了會幕。現在耶和華指示摩西，在會幕中當如何敬拜。

會幕（原文是「會見的帳幕」；見出27:21的注釋）是神宮殿在地上的象徵。至聖所裡的約櫃代表神的寶座（出40:1-33）。耶和華的榮光住在基路伯展開的翅膀之間，祂要在那裡與以色列人相會，向他們傳達祂的旨意（見出25:22）。

notes.en: When: This word introduces a major category (the process of presenting an offering), followed by a series of conditions introduced by if (1:3, 10, 14). This when/if pattern is generally followed through all the major offerings described in 1:2–6:7. • offering (Hebrew qorban; see study note on Mark 7:11) is a general term referring to all kinds of offerings and gifts, including the various offerings described in Lev 1–7.

notes.zh:
「若有人獻供物」：這句話先帶出一個大類別（獻上供物的程序），接著用一連串「若……」的條件分述不同情況（1:3、10、14）。1:2–6:7所描述的各種主要祭物，大致都按照這種先總說、再分項的寫法。

「供物」（希伯來文 qorban；見可7:11的注釋）是個統稱，指各種祭物和禮物，包括利未記1–7章所描述的各樣祭。

notes.en: burnt offering (Hebrew ‘olah, “what goes up”): The Hebrew word implies the ascent of the animal in flame and smoke. Except for its hide, given in payment to the officiating priest (7:8), this offering was burned completely on the altar (1:9). Its purpose was to satisfy God’s wrath against sin, ceremonially cleansing the worshiper and restoring him or her to fellowship with God (cp. Rom 3:25; 8:3; 2 Cor 5:18-21). The whole burnt offering occurs first in this list of offerings (Lev 1–7), providing a pattern for offerings that follow. It is the most common and most general atoning offering.

notes.zh: 「燔祭」（希伯來文 ‘olah，意思是「上升之物」）：這個希伯來字暗示祭牲隨著火焰和煙上升。燔祭除了皮歸給主禮的祭司（7:8）以外，要全部燒在壇上（1:9）。它的目的是平息神對罪的忿怒，在禮儀上潔淨獻祭的人，使他恢復與神的相交（參羅3:25；8:3；林後5:18-21）。燔祭在這一系列祭物（利1–7章）中排在第一，為後面各種祭立下模式；它是最常見、也最普遍的贖罪之祭。

notes.en: male with no defects: God allowed female and slightly deformed animals for certain types of non-atoning offerings (see 3:1; 4:27-31; 22:23), but not for the whole burnt offering. In the dry, brush-encrusted hills of southern Palestine, cattle were much more difficult to raise than sheep or goats. This meant a bull without defect was an animal of great value. Centuries later, the prophet Malachi confronted the people for offering sick and lame animals instead of those without defect (Mal 1:6-14).

notes.zh: 「沒有殘疾的公牛」：在某些不屬於贖罪的祭中，神容許用母畜或稍有缺陷的牲畜（見3:1；4:27-31；22:23），但燔祭不可以。在巴勒斯坦南部乾旱、長滿灌木的山地，養牛比養綿羊或山羊困難得多，所以一頭沒有殘疾的公牛非常貴重。幾百年後，先知瑪拉基就責備百姓用有病、瘸腿的牲畜，而不用沒有殘疾的來獻祭（瑪1:6-14）。

notes.en: Lay your hand on the animal’s head: The sacrificial animal represented the worshiper in the ceremony (4:4, 15, 24, 29, 33; 16:21). This act signified that the animal’s death represented the death of its owner. In the ritual for the Day of Atonement, it signified that the sins of the owner were transferred to the animal (16:20-22). With the peace offering (3:2, 8, 13), the act seems to have indicated ownership of the animal being sacrificed. • The phrase in your place may mean “in payment for sin” (sometimes called expiation) or “as a substitute for the sinner’s death” (sometimes called propitiation). • to purify you, making you right with him (or to make atonement for you): Although older commentaries describe this process as “covering over” sin, recent scholarship defines it as “blotting out, erasing, or cleansing from” sin. The concept involves satisfying God’s wrath against sin, ceremonially cleansing the worshiper, and restoring fellowship with God in the community of God’s people.

notes.zh:
「按手在燔祭牲的頭上」：在儀式中，祭牲代表獻祭的人（4:4、15、24、29、33；16:21）。這個動作表示：祭牲的死代表了牠主人的死。在贖罪日的儀式中，按手表示把主人的罪轉移到這隻牲畜身上（16:20-22）。在平安祭中（3:2、8、13），按手似乎是表明這隻祭牲屬於獻祭的人。

「燔祭便蒙悅納」：祭牲蒙悅納、代替獻祭的人，這可能是指為罪付上抵償，也可能是指代替罪人受死，平息神的忿怒。

「為他贖罪」：舊的注釋書常把這個過程解釋為把罪「遮蓋」起來，近年的研究則認為它的意思是把罪「塗抹、除去或洗淨」。這個觀念包括平息神對罪的忿怒、在禮儀上潔淨獻祭的人，並使他在神百姓的群體中恢復與神的相交。

notes.en: Aaron’s sons: The descendants of Levi, Moses’ own tribe, were divided into two categories: (1) priests, who were descendants of Aaron, the first high priest; and (2) Levites, who served in subordinate roles (Exod 28:1-4; Num 18:1-7). The instructions given here applied to later generations as well. • The blood was a symbol of life, not of death. The Israelite system of sacrifice was based on the principle of substitution, and the shedding of sacrificial blood was essential for atonement. It represented sacrificing the life of the animal as a substitute for the life of the worshiper (Lev 17:10-14; Heb 9:22). The blood of Jesus Christ was shed as the ultimate sacrifice for sin (Heb 9:11-14). • The altar of burnt offering was located in the east end of the courtyard, outside the Tabernacle but inside the entrance to the courtyard (Exod 40:6, 29).

notes.zh:
「亞倫子孫」：利未是摩西所屬的支派，利未的後代分成兩類：（1）祭司，是第一位大祭司亞倫的後代；（2）利未人，擔任協助的職務（出28:1-4；民18:1-7）。這裡的規定也適用於後來的世代。

血象徵生命，而不是死亡。以色列的獻祭制度建立在「代替」的原則上，流出祭牲的血是贖罪不可少的；它代表把祭牲的生命獻上，代替獻祭之人的生命（利17:10-14；來9:22）。耶穌基督流出祂的血，成為為罪所獻最終極的祭（來9:11-14）。

燔祭壇設在院子的東端，在會幕之外、院子入口之內（出40:6、29）。

notes.en: The entire animal was to be burned, except for the skin, which was the priest’s share of the offering (7:8).
notes.prepared: The entire animal was to be burned, except for the skin, which was the priest’s share of the offering (7:8).
notes.zh: 整隻祭牲都要焚燒，只有皮除外，皮是祭司從這祭中所得的一份（7:8）。

notes.en: The Hebrew word translated fat describes the suet, or hard fat, from around the kidneys and loins. This specific term occurs only here and in 1:12 and 8:20. All fat—not just this special fat—was considered God’s portion (3:14-17; 7:23-25; see 1 Sam 2:15-17). Only the whole burnt offering was entirely consumed on the altar. With other offerings, the fatty portions and certain internal organs were burned; the rest belonged to the officiating priests and sometimes to the worshiper (Lev 7:11-18).

notes.zh: 譯作「脂油」的希伯來字是指腰子和腰部周圍的板油（硬脂肪）。這個特定的字只出現在這裡和1:12、8:20。所有的脂油（不只是這種特別的脂油）都被視為歸給神的那一份（3:14-17；7:23-25；見撒上2:15-17）。只有燔祭是全部燒在壇上的；其他的祭只燒脂油和某些內臟，其餘的歸給主禮的祭司，有時也歸給獻祭的人（利7:11-18）。

notes.en: The offering was washed with water to remove dirt or debris that might contaminate the offering. Washing was also part of purification from ritual uncleanness, a prerequisite for Tabernacle service (6:27; 11:28). • special gift: The Hebrew term (’isheh) has traditionally been rendered “offering made by fire.” Although the offering was to be burned (1:13, 17), recent scholarship suggests that the word had the more generic meaning of “gift.” • pleasing aroma to the Lord (literally a restful odor; also in 1:13, 17): Pagan people of the ancient Near East believed that their gods smelled the offerings because they needed to eat them to sustain their lives. Although God’s response is sometimes represented in language that reflects the cultural setting (e.g., 21:6; Num 28:2), the Bible is clear that God did not need offerings as food (Ps 50:9-13). Instead, they pleased him as sincere offerings for the purpose of atonement.

notes.zh:
祭牲要用水洗，除去可能玷污祭物的塵土或雜物。洗濯也是潔淨禮儀上不潔的一部分，是在會幕中服事的先決條件（6:27；11:28）。

「火祭」：這個希伯來字（’isheh）傳統上譯作「用火獻的祭」。雖然這祭確實要焚燒（1:13、17），但近年的研究認為這個字的意思比較廣泛，指「禮物」。

「獻與耶和華為馨香」（原文是「安息的香氣」；又見1:13、17）：古代近東的異教徒相信，他們的神明聞得到祭物，因為神明需要吃祭物來維持生命。雖然聖經有時用反映當時文化背景的語言描述神的回應（例如21:6；民28:2），但聖經清楚表明，神並不需要祭物當作食物（詩50:9-13）。這些祭物蒙神喜悅，是因為它們是為了贖罪而真誠獻上的。

notes.en: Permission to offer lesser animals was to make the animal, and therefore atonement, more affordable to common Israelites. The method of offering these animals closely parallels the offering of bulls outlined in 1:3-9.

notes.zh: 容許獻較小的牲畜，是為了讓一般以色列人負擔得起祭牲，也就負擔得起贖罪。獻這些牲畜的方法，和1:3-9所說獻公牛的方法大致相同。

notes.en: Birds were plentiful, cheap, and easy to catch. This meant that atonement and worship through sacrifices were not only for the rich and privileged; the poor were also included (see also 5:7; 12:8; see Luke 2:24).

notes.zh: 鳥類數量多、價錢便宜，又容易捕捉。這表示藉著獻祭來贖罪和敬拜，不只是富人和有地位之人的專利，窮人也包括在內（又見5:7；12:8；見路2:24）。

notes.en: tear . . . without tearing it apart: Cutting larger animals into pieces (1:6, 12) probably reflects the ancient rite of covenant-making, in which the participant passed between the two halves of a sacrificed animal (see Gen 15:10). Because of their small size, birds were not cut in half. If it was necessary to pass between them, they were arranged in pairs.

excerpts.zh: 把鳥撕開，只是不可撕斷

notes.zh: 「把鳥撕開，只是不可撕斷」：把較大的牲畜切成塊子（1:6、12），可能反映古代立約的儀式，就是立約的人從切成兩半的祭牲中間經過（見創15:10）。鳥因為體型小，不切成兩半；若需要從中間經過，就把鳥成對擺放。

notes.en: The grain offering (Hebrew minkhah, “gift, present”) was a way to express worship to the Lord through a gift, recognizing him as Lord over the life of the worshiper. The grain offering was to accompany each whole burnt offering (Num 28:3-6, 12-13), sin offering (Num 6:14-15), and peace offering (Lev 9:4; Num 6:17). The grain offering supplied the priest with bread for his daily sustenance, because no farmland was allocated to priests.

notes.zh: 素祭（希伯來文 minkhah，意思是「禮物、贈禮」）是藉著獻上禮物來敬拜耶和華，承認祂是獻祭之人生命的主。每次獻燔祭（民28:3-6、12-13）、贖罪祭（民6:14-15）和平安祭（利9:4；民6:17），都要同時獻上素祭。素祭也供應祭司每日所需的餅，因為祭司沒有分到可以耕種的地業。

notes.en: Choice flour was fine wheat flour (in contrast with common barley flour). See also 1 Kgs 4:22; Ezek 16:13, 19. • Israelites used olive oil as shortening in their cooking, as lamp fuel, and for medicinal and cosmetic purposes. Accordingly, it was associated with the rich produce of the land and with God’s provision (Deut 8:8). • Like choice flour, frankincense was frequently connected with the Tabernacle (Exod 30:34; Lev 24:7) or the Temple (1 Chr 9:29). This fragrant tree resin was also used by individuals on special occasions (Song 3:6; Matt 2:11). It was a primary ingredient of the holy incense burned in the Holy Place as a tangible expression of worship (Exod 30:34-38).

notes.zh:
細麵是上好的麥子磨成的麵粉（相對於一般的大麥粉）。又見王上4:22；結16:13、19。

以色列人用橄欖油烹調食物、點燈，也作藥用和化妝用。因此橄欖油與這地豐富的出產和神的供應連在一起（申8:8）。

乳香和細麵一樣，常與會幕（出30:34；利24:7）或聖殿（代上9:29）有關。這種芬芳的樹脂也有人在特別的場合使用（歌3:6；太2:11）。它是在聖所中焚燒之聖香的主要成分，是具體表達敬拜的方式（出30:34-38）。

notes.en: The representative portion of the grain offering was burned on the altar to remind the worshiper that the whole offering belonged to God.

notes.zh: 把素祭中「作為紀念」的那一份燒在壇上，是提醒獻祭的人：整份祭物都屬於神。

notes.en: rest of the grain offering: A portion of the fire offerings was generally reserved for the priest as food (see 6:16-17). Exceptions included the whole burnt offering (the priest received only the hide; see 7:8), offerings given by the priest for himself (4:3-12; 6:19-23), or offerings made for the entire community (4:13-21). In these cases, the offering was to be entirely burned. The grain offering provided the priests with bread for their diet. • most holy (Hebrew qodesh qodashim, “holy of holies”): Both God and what belongs to him are holy. “Most holy” designates the priestly share as taken from the holy offering and reserved for a special function. This description is used for the priest’s share of any gifts dedicated to the Lord (Num 18:8-10).

notes.zh:
「素祭所剩的」：火祭中通常有一部分留給祭司作食物（見6:16-17）。例外的情形包括燔祭（祭司只得皮；見7:8）、祭司為自己獻的祭（4:3-12；6:19-23），以及為全會眾獻的祭（4:13-21）；這些祭要全部燒掉。素祭供應祭司日常所吃的餅。

「至聖」（希伯來文 qodesh qodashim，意思是「聖中之聖」）：神和屬於神的東西都是聖的。「至聖」是指祭司從聖祭中分得、留作特別用途的那一份。凡是獻給耶和華的禮物，祭司所得的那一份都用這個詞來形容（民18:8-10）。

notes.en: A large ceramic oven was placed in a hole, and around it a fire was kindled. Once the oven was hot, the flat bread baked against the inside of its wall. • without any yeast: See study note on 2:11; see also Exod 12:8.

「爐中烤」：古人把大型陶爐放在坑裡，在周圍生火；爐子燒熱後，把薄餅貼在爐的內壁上烤熟。

「無酵」：見2:11的注釋；又見出12:8。

notes.en: A griddle was a flat stone or clay surface propped above a fire and heated. Later griddles were made of metal (Ezek 4:3).

notes.en: yeast: The bread commonly eaten in biblical times was comparable to modern sourdough. The substance that is often called “leaven” consisted of wild yeast spores mixed into moist dough or a flour mixture. The yeast would grow and cause the dough to ferment, souring and raising it. A reserved portion of the sour dough would be kneaded into subsequent batches (Matt 13:33). Unleavened bread was required for the Passover (Exod 12:8), in remembrance of Israel’s bondage in Egypt (Deut 16:3) and their speedy departure from that land (Exod 12:34; 13:3). Following the Exodus, unleavened bread acquired the status of altar bread. Leavened bread was not to be burned on the altar. • honey: The Hebrew word (debash) can also refer to fruit nectar. The reason for its exclusion is not stated, but perhaps the frequent use of honey in pagan offerings, particularly to gods of the underworld, was a contributing reason. If the word refers to fruit nectar, its association with wine and fermentation may have linked it with yeast, making it ineligible to be burned on the altar. However, both honey and yeast were allowed as part of an offering of first crops (Lev 2:12). Loaves of bread made with yeast were to be presented with thank offerings (7:13) and as a gift to the priest in the Festival of Harvest (23:17). In the New Testament, yeast becomes a spiritual metaphor, playing on its sour taste and on its tendency to spread (Matt 16:6, 11, 12; 1 Cor 5:6-8; cp. Matt 13:33).

notes.zh:
「酵」：聖經時代人們平常吃的餅類似今天的酸種麵包。常被稱為「酵」的東西，其實是混在濕麵團或麵粉糊中的野生酵母。酵母繁殖後，使麵團發酵、變酸、膨脹。人們會留下一部分酸麵團，揉進下一批麵團裡（太13:33）。逾越節必須吃無酵餅（出12:8），為要記念以色列人在埃及為奴（申16:3），以及他們匆忙離開那地（出12:34；13:3）。出埃及之後，無酵餅成了壇上專用的餅；有酵的餅不可燒在壇上。

「蜜」：這個希伯來字（debash）也可以指果汁熬成的糖漿。經文沒有說明為什麼不可獻蜜，或許部分原因是異教的祭祀（特別是獻給陰間神明的祭）常常用蜜。如果這個字指果汁糖漿，它與酒和發酵的關聯，可能使它被視為和酵同類，因此不可燒在壇上。不過，獻初熟之物時，蜜和酵都可以作為供物的一部分（利2:12）。獻感謝祭時要同獻有酵的餅（7:13），在七七節也要把有酵的餅作為禮物獻給祭司（23:17）。在新約中，酵成了屬靈的比喻，取它味道酸和容易擴散的特性（太16:6、11、12；林前5:6-8；參太13:33）。

notes.en: offering of the first crops: This offering (called “firstfruits” in many translations) was brought from the first part of the harvest (23:15-21; Num 28:26-31). Like the representative portion of the grain offering, this offering acknowledged that the entire harvest belonged to God (Lev 23:10-11; Exod 22:29; 23:19; 34:26; Num 15:18-20; Deut 18:4-5; 26:1-2). It further recognized that the land itself, not just its products, belonged to God; Israel was merely the tenant (see Lev 25:23).

notes.zh: 「初熟的供物」：這供物（許多譯本作「初熟之果」）是從收成的第一部分拿來的（23:15-21；民28:26-31）。如同素祭中作為紀念的一份，這供物承認全部的收成都屬於神（利23:10-11；出22:29；23:19；34:26；民15:18-20；申18:4-5；26:1-2）。它更進一步承認，不只是地的出產，連土地本身也屬於神；以色列人在神面前只是寄居的（見利25:23）。

notes.en: In ancient times, salt represented permanence because it preserved food. A covenant of salt (see study notes on Num 18:19; 2 Chr 13:5) denoted an enduring covenant that was renewed with successive generations.
notes.prepared: In ancient times, salt represented permanence because it preserved food. A covenant of salt (見民18:19、代下13:5的注釋) denoted an enduring covenant that was renewed with successive generations.
notes.zh: 在古代，鹽能保存食物，因此象徵恆久不變。「立約的鹽」（見民18:19；代下13:5的注釋）表示一個持久、代代更新的約。

notes.en: The peace offering (Hebrew shelem) expressed worship through fellowship with the Lord and with others. The Hebrew word is from the same root as shalom, which speaks of wholeness, well-being, harmony, and peace. Shalom means more than a cessation of hostilities between God and the worshiper; it implies a bond of harmonious fellowship. The peace offering was therefore a shared meal celebrating fellowship with God and others (cp. Exod 18:12; 24:9-11; 1 Sam 9:15-24). It could be presented as an expression of thanks (Lev 7:12-15), as a voluntary offering, or in fulfillment of a vow (7:16-18; 22:21). Peace offerings often followed whole burnt offerings (e.g., 1 Kgs 9:25), showing that fellowship with God follows atonement. When we have experienced atonement through Christ, we are able to be at peace with God and with each other (see Acts 2:42; 10:36; Rom 5:1; 1 Cor 10:16; 11:17-34; 2 Cor 5:18-21).

notes.zh: 平安祭（希伯來文 shelem）是藉著與耶和華、與眾人相交來表達敬拜。這個希伯來字和 shalom 同一個字根，含有完整、安康、和諧、平安的意思。Shalom 不只是神與敬拜者之間停止敵對，更是一種和睦相交的關係。所以平安祭是一頓共享的筵席，慶祝與神、與人的相交（參出18:12；24:9-11；撒上9:15-24）。平安祭可以為表達感謝而獻（利7:12-15），也可以是甘心獻的祭，或為還願而獻（7:16-18；22:21）。平安祭常接在燔祭之後獻上（例如王上9:25），表明先有贖罪，才有與神的相交。我們藉著基督得蒙救贖，就能與神和好，彼此和睦（見徒2:42；10:36；羅5:1；林前10:16；11:17-34；林後5:18-21）。

notes.en: a male or a female: The whole burnt offering allowed only the use of male animals because it made atonement (1:3, 10). The less formal peace offering permitted both male and female animals (see also 4:28, 32). • no defects: The sacrificial animals had to be healthy. The only exception was the voluntary offering, for which a slight blemish was permissible (22:23).

「無論是公的是母的」：燔祭只能用公的牲畜，因為它是為了贖罪（1:3、10）。比較不那麼正式的平安祭，公的母的都可以（又見4:28、32）。

「沒有殘疾」：祭牲必須健康。唯一的例外是甘心祭，可以有輕微的缺陷（22:23）。

notes.en: kidneys . . . lobe of the liver: The Israelites saw the kidneys as organs of understanding, much like how we think of the brain (“I am overwhelmed [literally my kidneys are consumed],” Job 19:27; “heart,” Pss 7:9; 16:7; Jer 12:2; Lam 3:13; “motives,” Ps 26:2; Jer 17:10; “thoughts,” Jer 11:20; 20:12). The liver represented life and vitality, similar to how we think of the heart (Prov 7:23; “spirit,” Lam 2:11).

notes.zh: 「腰子……肝上的網子」：以色列人把腰子看作理解和心思的器官，就像我們今天說「頭腦」一樣；和合本常把這個字譯作「心腸」或「肺腑」（伯19:27；詩7:9；16:7；26:2；耶11:20；12:2；17:10；20:12；哀3:13）。肝代表生命和活力，就像我們今天說「心」一樣（箴7:23「直等箭穿他的肝」；哀2:11「我的肝膽塗地」）。

notes.en: The burnt offering is described in 1:3-17 and is best referred to as the “whole burnt offering.” Because it was offered twice daily (see Num 28:4), and because the need for atonement preceded fellowship, the text assumes that the burnt offering would be on the altar already. The priest was to lay the fatty portions and certain internal organs (3:3-4) of the peace offering on top of it.

notes.en: Sheep were smaller, easier to raise, and less expensive than cattle. Apart from the exceptions mentioned in these verses, offerings of sheep followed the same pattern as those of cattle.

notes.en: broad tail: Sheep in this part of the ancient Near East had broad, fatty tails that were burned on the altar with the rest of the fat.

notes.zh: 「整肥尾巴」：古代近東這一帶的綿羊有又寬又肥的尾巴，要和其他脂油一起燒在壇上。

notes.en: special gift: See study note on 1:9. • Offerings of food were called “God’s food” (21:6, 8, 17, 21, 22; Num 28:2). However, Scripture is clear that the Lord did not eat the offerings, as pagans believed their deities did (Ps 50:9-13). Instead, these offerings belonged to God, and the priest ate a portion of this food as God’s representative (Lev 21:21-22). These offerings sustained the priest and his family.

「為食物」：獻給神的祭物被稱為「神的食物」（21:6、8、17、21、22；民28:2）。然而聖經清楚表明，耶和華並不吃祭物，不像異教徒以為他們的神明會吃（詩50:9-13）。這些祭物屬於神，祭司代表神吃其中的一部分（利21:21-22）。這些祭物供養了祭司和他的家人。

notes.en: The offering of goats followed a similar pattern as for cattle and sheep. Both goats and sheep were considered offerings from the flock (see 3:6).

notes.en: Human beings were not permitted to eat the fat or blood (see 1:5, 8 and study notes).

notes.en: The sin offering (Hebrew khatta’t, from the root khata’, meaning “to lack, fall short, miss, fail”) was for specific unintentional violations of God’s commands (see also Num 15:22-29), intended to repair a loss or remedy a failure (e.g., Lev 5:1-4). Although we all sin, God will forgive us if we confess it (Gal 6:1; 1 Jn 1:8-9). But we are warned against sinning “brazenly” or “deliberately” (Num 15:30-31; Heb 6:4-6; 10:26-29).

notes.zh: 贖罪祭（希伯來文 khatta’t，字根 khata’ 的意思是「缺少、達不到、射不中、失敗」）是為了無意中違反神某些特定的命令而獻的（又見民15:22-29），目的是彌補虧欠或補救過失（例如利5:1-4）。我們都會犯罪，但我們若認自己的罪，神必赦免我們（加6:1；約壹1:8-9）。然而聖經也警告我們，不可「擅敢」或「故意」犯罪（民15:30-31；來6:4-6；10:26-29）。

notes.en: These verses distinguish two types of sin offerings: (1) the offering given for the sin of the high priest (4:3, 20) and the entire Israelite community (4:13), and (2) the offering given for one of Israel’s leaders (4:22) and any of the common people (4:27). The former case required offering a bull, a large, expensive animal. It was not to be eaten (6:30) but was completely burned (4:12, 21), and some of its blood was presented in the Holy Place (4:6-7, 17-18). The latter case required a lesser animal—a male goat for a lay leader or a female sheep or goat for a common person. The priest ate a portion of the layperson’s offering (6:24-29), and the blood was presented at the bronze altar in the courtyard (4:25, 30). The distinction stresses the responsibilities of leaders. The offering was the same for the priest as for the entire people, and the lay leader’s offering was more than that of a common person. The New Testament also emphasizes the responsibility of religious leaders; those who teach (Jas 3:1) and those who serve as religious leaders (Matt 23:1-33; Luke 20:47) are judged more severely than those who follow them.

The offering was the same for the priest as for the entire people, and the lay leader’s offering was more than that of a common person. The New Testament also emphasizes the responsibility of religious leaders; those who teach (雅3:1) and those who serve as religious leaders (太23:1-33; 路20:47) are judged more severely than those who follow them.
notes.zh: 這幾節區分兩類贖罪祭：（1）為大祭司（4:3、20）和以色列全會眾（4:13）的罪所獻的；（2）為以色列的官長（4:22）和一般百姓（4:27）所獻的。前一類要獻公牛，是體型大、價錢高的牲畜；這祭不可吃（6:30），要全部燒掉（4:12、21），還要把一些血帶進聖所（4:6-7、17-18）。後一類用較小的牲畜：官長獻公山羊，一般百姓獻母山羊或母綿羊。祭司可以吃一般人所獻之祭的一部分（6:24-29），血則在院子裡的銅壇處理（4:25、30）。這樣的區分強調了領袖的責任：祭司所獻的與全會眾所獻的相同，官長所獻的又比一般百姓多。新約同樣強調宗教領袖的責任：作師傅的（雅3:1）和作宗教領袖的（太23:1-33；路20:47），要比跟從他們的人受更重的審判。

notes.en: The high priest was designated by God and “anointed” (Hebrew mashiakh, “set apart by the ritual of anointing”) for a particular service. In 1 Sam 1:1—2 Kgs 25:30, anointing most often refers to Israel’s king (see 1 Sam 24:6; 2 Sam 1:14; 19:21). While all priests were anointed (Exod 40:13-15), here the term probably refers to the high priest because he was specially anointed for service in the Tabernacle (Lev 6:20; 8:12). Since the high priest was mediator for all of Israel, including lesser priests, his sin would bring guilt on the entire assembly (see “Community Identity” Theme Note). • Guilt results from violating God’s will; it is not just perceived or psychological guilt (see study note on 5:17-19).

notes.zh:
「受膏的祭司」：大祭司是神所指定、「受膏」（希伯來文 mashiakh，意思是「藉著膏抹的儀式分別出來」）擔任特定職分的人。在撒上1:1—王下25:30，「受膏者」大多指以色列的王（見撒上24:6；撒下1:14；19:21）。雖然所有的祭司都受了膏（出40:13-15），但這裡可能是指大祭司，因為他特別受膏在會幕中供職（利6:20；8:12）。大祭司是全以色列（包括其他祭司）的中保，所以他犯罪會使全會眾都擔罪責（「使百姓陷在罪裏」）。

罪責是因違背神的旨意而產生的，不只是自己感覺有罪或心理上的罪疚感（見5:17-19的注釋）。

notes.en: The Tabernacle complex had a tent (sometimes called the “Tent of Meeting”; see study note on 1:1) at the west end of the courtyard. Inside the tent, the inner curtain divided the first room, the Holy Place, from the second, the Most Holy Place. The Most Holy Place contained the Ark of the Covenant (Exod 26:31-33) and was God’s throne room (see study note on Lev 1:1). Sprinkling the animal’s blood before the curtain (4:6, 17) and applying it to the horns of the incense altar (4:7, 18) was done to atone for the anointed priest or for the entire congregation. This action demonstrated the gravity of the offenses being atoned for (cp. 4:25, 30-35).

notes.zh: 會幕的範圍包括院子西端的一座帳幕（就是狹義的「會幕」；見1:1的注釋）。帳幕裡面，內層的幔子把第一間（聖所）和第二間（至聖所）隔開。至聖所裡有約櫃（出26:31-33），是神的寶座所在（見利1:1的注釋）。對著幔子彈血（4:6、17），並把血抹在香壇的四角上（4:7、18），是為受膏的祭司或全會眾贖罪。這樣做顯示所要贖的罪過有多嚴重（參4:25、30-35）。

notes.en: The altar for fragrant incense stood in front of the inner curtain, just outside the Most Holy Place (4:6). It had four protrusions resembling horns, as did the altar for burnt offerings (see study note on Exod 27:2). The priests burned incense on this altar to the Lord each morning and evening (Exod 30:1-10).

notes.zh: 香壇立在內層幔子前面，就在至聖所外（4:6）。香壇和燔祭壇一樣，四角有像角一樣凸出的部分（見出27:2的注釋）。祭司每天早晚在這壇上向耶和華燒香（出30:1-10）。

notes.en: Only the offerings for the priest or the entire community were burned outside the camp. Perhaps this was commanded because the offering had figuratively absorbed the contamination of the high priest or the community and therefore had to be disposed of outside the camp. Those guilty were not to partake of or reap any benefit from their own sin offerings, even if they were priests (6:19-23).

notes.zh: 只有為祭司或全會眾所獻的祭，才要搬到營外焚燒。這樣規定，或許是因為這祭物在象徵上吸收了大祭司或會眾的污穢，所以必須在營外處理。犯罪的人不可吃自己所獻的贖罪祭，也不可從中得任何好處，即使他是祭司也一樣（6:19-23）。

notes.en: The Hebrew term for elders is related to the word for beard. It implies mature but not necessarily elderly individuals. They were leaders of the community—typically, heads of families and tribes (cp. Exod 18:21-26; Deut 22:15-19). For this offering, the elders represented the entire people, as they would later in anointing David as king (2 Sam 5:3).

notes.zh: 譯作「長老」的希伯來字和「鬍鬚」有關，指成熟的人，不一定是年老的。長老是群體的領袖，通常是家族和支派的首領（參出18:21-26；申22:15-19）。在這祭中，長老代表全體百姓，就像後來他們代表百姓膏大衛作王一樣（撒下5:3）。

notes.en: A similar form of the phrase they will be forgiven appears frequently in passages dealing with atonement (4:26, 31, 35; 5:10, 13, 16, 18; 6:7; 19:22; Num 15:25, 26, 28). God is willing to forgive a repentant person’s sin and restore him or her to the community of faith.

notes.zh: 「他們必蒙赦免」：類似的說法常出現在論到贖罪的經文中（4:26、31、35；5:10、13、16、18；6:7；19:22；民15:25、26、28）。神願意赦免悔改之人的罪，使他重新回到信仰的群體中。

notes.en: The sin offerings described in this passage atoned for laypersons, whether leaders or other Israelite citizens. These offerings could be eaten (contrast 4:3-21), and they involved lesser animals. The blood of the offering was disposed of in the courtyard of the Tabernacle and not carried to the Holy Place. As with the peace offering (ch 3), the fat and certain internal organs were burned on the altar. However, the rest of the meat from these offerings was given to the priest as food for himself and the males in his family (6:29), and it was to be eaten in a holy place (6:26; cp. 10:16-20). A lay leader was to offer a male goat (4:23), while a common layperson could offer a female goat or lamb. The animal’s lesser size and cost reflected the lesser influence of the common Israelite and, probably, their financial situation. Economic considerations allowed those who were poor to bring a pair of doves or young pigeons (5:7-8; 12:6, 8; cp. Luke 2:24). The desperately poor could offer two quarts of flour (Lev 5:11).

notes.zh: 這段經文所說的贖罪祭，是為一般人（無論是官長或其他以色列百姓）贖罪的。這些祭可以吃（與4:3-21不同），用的牲畜也比較小。祭牲的血在會幕的院子裡處理，不帶進聖所。和平安祭（第3章）一樣，脂油和某些內臟要燒在壇上；不過這些祭其餘的肉要歸給祭司，作他和他家中男丁的食物（6:29），而且要在聖處吃（6:26；參10:16-20）。官長要獻公山羊（4:23），一般百姓則可以獻母山羊或羊羔。牲畜較小、價錢較低，反映出一般以色列人的影響力較小，可能也考慮到他們的經濟能力。窮人可以帶兩隻斑鳩或兩隻雛鴿來（5:7-8；12:6、8；參路2:24）；極其貧窮的人可以獻細麵伊法十分之一（約兩公升；利5:11）。

notes.en: Israel’s leaders included the elders (see 4:15), tribal heads, and family heads (see Num 1:16, 44; 1 Kgs 8:1).

notes.zh: 「血……抹在燔祭壇的四角上」：官長（4:25）或一般百姓（4:30、34）所獻之祭的血，和為祭司獻的公牛的血不同，不可帶進聖所。此外，獻這祭的祭司要吃其中一部分的肉（6:24-29）。

notes.en: The common people, who had less responsibility than a priest or leader, were permitted the lesser offering of a female sheep or goat. A greater position brings greater responsibility (cp. Amos 3:2; Matt 25:14-30; Jas 3:1).

notes.en: These verses list examples of sins covered by the sin offering (4:2). When a person realized he or she had committed an offense, the next step was to make it right by admitting guilt and bringing a sin offering.

notes.en: The first infraction was the failure to testify when called as a witness before a court. Failure to testify was not a passive act because it actively aided the criminal. • you will be punished (literally you become guilty or you realize your guilt): Anticipating God’s punishment for the sin, the guilty party offered the sacrifice to remove the guilt and escape the punishment.

第一種過犯是在法庭上被傳作見證時不肯作證。不作證並不是消極的不作為，因為它實際上是在幫助犯罪的人。

「他要擔當他的罪孽」：犯罪的人預料神會因這罪懲罰他，所以獻上祭物，為要除去罪責、免受懲罰。

notes.en: ceremonially unclean: “Clean” and “unclean” did not pertain to hygiene (see 11:1–15:33) but to suitability for participating in worship or, in the case of animals, suitability for sacrifice or human consumption. A list of clean and unclean animals is found in 11:1-47. The requirement for becoming clean after touching an unclean animal was merely to wash one’s clothes and remain apart from the community until evening (11:25). Most likely, therefore, the requirement of this sin offering indicates that the person had failed to follow the prescription for cleansing (11:27-28).

notes.zh: 「不潔」：「潔淨」和「不潔」與衛生無關（見11:1–15:33），而是指一個人是否適合參與敬拜；若是指動物，則是指是否適合獻祭或給人吃。潔淨與不潔之動物的清單記在11:1-47。摸了不潔的動物之後，要成為潔淨，只需要洗衣服，並且不潔淨到晚上（11:25）。因此，這裡要求獻贖罪祭，最可能是因為這人沒有遵行潔淨的規定（11:27-28）。

notes.en: Any bodily discharge, even blood, would render a person temporarily unclean (chs 11–15). The uncleanness itself was not sin, but it was a sin to neglect the uncleanness, allowing it to spread. Once people became aware of their unclean state, they were guilty if they neglected it.

notes.en: Oaths could be taken in the name of the Lord. However, a foolish vow, one thoughtlessly made, was a blasphemous misuse of the Lord’s name (Exod 20:7). Accordingly, vows must be fulfilled (see Num 30:2; Deut 23:21-23; Eccl 5:4-6).

notes.zh: 人可以奉耶和華的名起誓。然而愚昧、輕率所發的誓，就是褻瀆地妄稱耶和華的名（出20:7）。因此，許了願就必須還（見民30:2；申23:21-23；傳5:4-6）。

notes.en: When you become aware of your guilt: All the situations that required a sin offering assumed guilt by accident or ignorance. As soon as a person became aware of having done something improper, he or she became guilty and was required to attend to it. Known sins were to be dealt with; it was a sin in itself to know what was right and not do it (see 5:17; Jas 4:17). • confess: Sacrifice for sin without admission of guilt would be a meaningless ritual. When the sacrificial animal was presented to the priest, the worshiper likely told the priest why it was being offered.

notes.zh:
「他有了罪的時候」：所有需要獻贖罪祭的情況，都是假設人因意外或無知而犯罪。一旦發覺自己做了不當的事，他就有了罪，必須處理。已知的罪必須處理；知道該行善卻不去行，這本身就是罪（見5:17；雅4:17）。

「承認」：獻祭贖罪卻不承認罪過，就只是毫無意義的儀式。人把祭牲帶到祭司面前時，可能會告訴祭司獻這祭的原因。

notes.en: The penalty was apparently fulfilled by the required sacrifice (see study note on 4:1–5:13). • The actions described in 5:1-5 best fit those of a layperson, so a female offering was permitted, in keeping with the principle demonstrated in 4:28, 32.

Although an animal offering was typically required for atonement (17:11), God in his grace allowed the bloodless offering of flour if the worshiper could not even afford two birds (5:11).

notes.en: The guilt offering (Hebrew ’asham, “guilt”) dealt with property loss and damages, whether sacred (5:14-16) or secular (6:1-7). It involved restitution as well as compensation for the loss (5:16; 6:5). It could be called a “penalty offering,” because the ram was a penalty, or perhaps a “restitution offering,” because of the need to make restitution for the loss before the ram was offered. In the guilt offering (5:14–6:7), the loss involved was not only a failure in God’s sight, as with the sin offering, but also a loss of property to another person or to the sanctuary. Cp. Matt 5:23-24.

notes.zh: 贖愆祭（希伯來文 ’asham，意思是「罪責」）處理財物的損失和損害，無論是聖物（5:14-16）或一般的財物（6:1-7）。它包括歸還原物，並賠償損失（5:16；6:5）。這祭可以稱為「罰金祭」，因為所獻的公綿羊就是罰金；也可以稱為「賠償祭」，因為獻公綿羊之前，必須先賠償損失。在贖愆祭（5:14–6:7）中，所涉及的不只是像贖罪祭那樣在神眼中的虧欠，還使別人或聖所蒙受財物的損失。參太5:23-24。

notes.en: unintentionally defiling: Damage to sacred property was distinguished from damage to secular property. The sacrifice was effective only if the damage to sacred property had been committed accidentally. Deliberate damage, such as vandalism, to something sacred was blasphemous. As with other deliberate sins (Num 15:30-31), no means was specified for its atonement. No devout believer would defiantly continue in sin (see 1 Jn 3:9). • The sanctuary shekel was not a coin but a standardized unit for measuring weight. It was used to evaluate the ram being offered. Some scholars suggest that this text permits the substitution of the appropriate amount of silver for the ram.

excerpts.zh: 在耶和華的聖物上誤犯了罪

notes.zh:
「在耶和華的聖物上誤犯了罪」：損害聖物和損害一般財物是有區分的。損害聖物的情況，只有在出於無意時，獻祭才有效。故意損害聖物（例如蓄意破壞）是褻瀆的行為；和其他故意的罪一樣（民15:30-31），律法沒有規定贖罪的方法。真正敬虔的信徒不會悖逆地繼續犯罪（見約壹3:9）。

「聖所的舍客勒」不是錢幣，而是標準的重量單位，用來估定所獻公綿羊的價值。有些學者認為，這段經文容許用等值的銀子代替公綿羊。

notes.en: The surcharge of an additional 20 percent provided compensation to the owner for loss or damage to property. The surcharge for sacred property was paid directly to the priests. Accidental damage to sacred property occurred when a person unintentionally ate the sacred offerings (22:14) or omitted the tithe (27:31). A similar surcharge was involved in redeeming an animal (27:13, 27).

notes.en: This paragraph provides general principles for the guilt offering. Even if unaware of the infraction, an individual was guilty and had to provide the appropriate guilt offering. This applied to both sacred and secular property (5:14-16; 6:1-7).

notes.en: sins against your associate . . . unfaithful to the Lord: For believers, there really is no such thing as a “secular” sin. All sin involves God, even sin directed against another person or group. In the sins requiring a guilt offering, God’s forgiveness was needed, but restitution to the injured individual had to be made first (6:5-7; cp. Matt 5:23-24). Unlike offenses against sacred property (Lev 5:14-16), both accidental and intentional offenses against secular property could be forgiven.

notes.en: The regulations in 1:2–6:7 include instructions for both priest and layperson. This section adds detail regarding the rights and obligations of the officiating priest. Because the tribe of Levi had been allotted no land for farming (Deut 18:1; Josh 13:14, 33), priests depended on the offering system for their income. The concern was that priests be adequately provided for. Like many human institutions, this system was eventually abused (1 Sam 2:12-25; Hos 4:8).

notes.en: The priest was required to wear official linen clothing, the attire of his office, when officiating at the Tabernacle. notes.en: cut off: Three interpretations are possible for this expression, all of them very grave: (1) The person was subject to God’s judgment and faced an early death by natural causes (17:10-14). (2) The person was to be executed by the community (cp. Exod 31:14). (3) The person lost communal membership in Israel, either by banishment (such as by excommunication) or by shunning the person and treating him or her as unclean (Lev 18:24-30; cp. 23:29-30, where “cut off” seems distinct from “destroy”).

notes.zh: 「從民中剪除」：這個說法可能有三種解釋，都非常嚴重：（1）這人要受神的審判，因自然因素而早死（17:10-14）；（2）這人要被群體處死（參出31:14）；（3）這人失去在以色列群體中的身分，或是被驅逐（例如逐出會眾），或是被人迴避、被當作不潔的人看待（利18:24-30；參23:29-30，那裡的「剪除」似乎與「滅絕」不同）。

notes.en: In the sacrificial system, the fat and blood of all altar offerings belonged to God. They were offered before any of the sacrifice could be eaten. Consuming blood was specifically forbidden because it represented the very life of the animal (17:10-16). The injunction against eating fat might have been because fat, considered to be the best part of the offering, belonged to God.

notes.zh: 在獻祭制度中，一切壇上祭物的脂油和血都屬於神，要在祭物任何部分被人吃之前先獻上。吃血是明文禁止的，因為血代表牲畜的生命（17:10-16）。禁止吃脂油，或許是因為脂油被視為祭物中最好的部分，是屬於神的。

notes.en: Animals found dead had not been drained of their blood and were therefore unclean. Their fat was unfit to offer to the Lord and could not be eaten. However, it could be used for any other purpose, such as greasing cart axles, waterproofing animal hides, and other household uses.

notes.en: The prohibition against consuming blood was so important that the Council at Jerusalem included it in the instructions for Gentile believers (Acts 15:29).

notes.zh: 禁止吃血的規定非常重要，耶路撒冷大會甚至把它列入給外邦信徒的指示中（徒15:29）。

notes.en: breast of the special offering . . . right thigh of the sacred offering: The peace offering was a shared meal between God, the priest, the worshiper, and guests. The breast (in some older translations called a “wave offering”) and thigh (sometimes called the “contribution” or “heave offering”) were specifically designated as the priest’s portion (see 10:13-15). After these offerings were taken into the Tabernacle and presented before the Lord, they could then be eaten (see Exod 29:24, 26).

notes.zh: 「搖的胸」……「舉的腿」：平安祭是神、祭司、敬拜者和客人共享的筵席。胸（「搖祭」）和右腿（「舉祭」）特別指定歸給祭司（見10:13-15）。這些祭物帶進會幕、在耶和華面前獻上之後，就可以吃（見出29:24、26）。

notes.en: In Exod 28–29, the Lord gave Moses specific instructions for clothing and for ordaining Aaron and his sons as priests. In Exod 39:1-31; 40:12-16; and Lev 8, the commands were carried out. Moses didn’t just pass along the instructions verbally; he enacted the rituals to provide an example for the priests down to the last detail, just as the Lord had commanded him (8:9, 13, 17, 21, 29). Because the penalty for disobedience was death, God made sure the priests knew exactly what to do.

notes.zh: 在出埃及記28–29章，耶和華指示摩西如何為亞倫和他的兒子做聖衣，並立他們作祭司；出39:1-31；40:12-16和利未記第8章記載這些命令被執行出來。摩西不只是口頭轉達指示，他親自執行這些儀式，為祭司立下榜樣，連最細微的地方都照著耶和華所吩咐他的去做（8:9、13、17、21、29）。因為違背命令的刑罰是死，神要確保祭司清楚知道該怎麼做。

notes.en: Being washed . . . with water was the first step for cleansing from impurity. The priests had to be ceremonially clean before they could serve the Lord in holiness (Exod 29:4; see Ps 24:4).

notes.zh: 「用水洗」是除去不潔的第一步。祭司必須在禮儀上潔淨，才能以聖潔事奉耶和華（出29:4；見詩24:4）。

notes.en: The tunic (see Exod 28:39) was woven of patterned linen cloth. • The same type of material used for the Tabernacle curtains was used for the embroidered ephod (see Exod 28:4, 6-14). This garment’s precise shape and size are unclear, but it seems to have been a long, sleeveless vest, fitted close to the body and tied about the waist. It was joined at the shoulders by gold settings; each setting bore an onyx stone engraved with the names of six of the tribes of Israel (Exod 28:9). Later, an ephod also referred to a venerated image (Judg 8:27; 18:17). • The decorative sash was embroidered and was made of the same materials as the ephod (see Exod 28:8).

notes.zh:
「內袍」（見出28:39）是用有花紋的細麻布織成的。

繡花的「以弗得」用的是和會幕幔子相同的材料（見出28:4、6-14）。這件衣服確切的形狀和大小不清楚，但它似乎是一件長而無袖的背心，貼身穿著，在腰間繫住。以弗得的兩肩各有金槽，鑲著一塊紅瑪瑙，上面刻著以色列六個支派的名字（出28:9）。後來，「以弗得」也指一種受人崇拜的像（士8:27；18:17）。

「巧工織的帶子」是繡花的，用和以弗得相同的材料做成（見出28:8）。

notes.en: The chestpiece (see Exod 28:15-30) was made of embroidered linen folded double. It bore twelve stones, each engraved with the name of a tribe of Israel. It was suspended over the heart by a gold chain from the gold shoulder-pieces of the ephod. • The Urim and the Thummim were placed in the pocket of the chestpiece (Exod 28:30; 1 Sam 23:9-12; 30:7-8); the precise function of these items is uncertain. They are generally thought of as two stones, perhaps each different in color, that were cast as lots. They apparently could give a positive, neutral, or negative answer to questions that could not otherwise be resolved (Exod 28:30; Num 27:21; 1 Sam 28:6). Their mention in Old Testament prophetic literature written centuries later (Ezra 2:63; Neh 7:65) demonstrates how important these items were to the office of priest.

notes.zh:
「胸牌」（見出28:15-30）是用繡花的細麻布雙層摺成的，上面有十二塊寶石，每塊刻著以色列一個支派的名字。胸牌用金鍊子從以弗得的金肩帶上掛下來，垂在心口。

「烏陵和土明」放在胸牌的袋中（出28:30；撒上23:9-12；30:7-8）；它們確切的作用並不清楚。一般認為它們是兩塊石頭，或許顏色不同，用來抽籤。它們似乎可以對其他方法無法解決的問題，給出肯定、中性或否定的答案（出28:30；民27:21；撒上28:6）。幾百年後寫成的舊約經卷仍提到它們（拉2:63；尼7:65），可見這些物件對祭司職分是多麼重要。

notes.en: The turban worn by the high priest was made of linen and was distinct from the headdresses of the common priests (Exod 28:40). The gold medallion was suspended from the turban and bore an inscription that read, “Holy to the Lord” (Exod 28:36). With the names of the tribes on his shoulders and over his heart and the dedication to the Lord on his forehead, the high priest was clearly marked as the people’s representative to God and God’s representative to the people. In this mediating role, the high priest modeled the standard for all priests.

notes.en: making them holy: God is the Holy One (Pss 22:3; 78:41). In the strictest sense, only God can make a person or thing holy (Lev 20:8; 21:15, 23; 22:9, 16, 32; Exod 31:13; see Heb 2:11); the actions of Moses simply recognized and declared what God had done (also in Lev 8:11, 12, 15).

notes.en: Aaron’s [ear]lobe, thumb, and big toe represented his total person. This act emphasized the role of the priestly office, with the blood stressing the ties to the sacrificial system. The priest’s basic function was mediation between God and his people. To do this effectively, he needed ears that could hear the words of God and the needs of his people, hands ready to do God’s bidding, and feet ready to take him where he was needed.

notes.en: seven days: This command emphasized God’s absolute holiness and mandated strict compliance with his commands. The priests, now anointed as God’s holy servants, were to remain in the Tabernacle court for seven days before venturing out into everyday life.

notes.en: Just as holiness describes God’s person and nature, the glory of the Lord tangibly expresses his power and majesty (see Ezek 1:28; 10:4). His glory was revealed on Mount Sinai (Exod 24:16), at the dedication of the Tabernacle (Exod 40:34-35), and in Solomon’s Temple (1 Kgs 8:11; 2 Chr 7:1). Yet it remained as vast as the heavens (Ps 19:1). The New Testament speaks of Christ’s glory as the image of God (2 Cor 4:4), who manifested God’s glory to the world (John 1:14). He was glorified in his death and resurrection (John 17:1-5). See also Exod 24:15-17.

The New Testament speaks of Christ’s glory as the image of God (林後4:4), who manifested God’s glory to the world (約1:14). He was glorified in his death and resurrection (約17:1-5). See also 出24:15-17.
notes.zh: 聖潔描述神的位格和本性，「耶和華的榮光」則具體地彰顯祂的能力和威嚴（見結1:28；10:4）。祂的榮光曾在西奈山（出24:16）、會幕奉獻時（出40:34-35）和所羅門的聖殿中（王上8:11；代下7:1）顯現，卻仍然像諸天一樣浩大（詩19:1）。新約說，基督的榮光是神的像（林後4:4），祂向世人彰顯了神的榮耀（約1:14），並在祂的死和復活中得了榮耀（約17:1-5）。又見出24:15-17。

notes.en: Aaron’s two older sons, Nadab and Abihu (Exod 6:23), had accompanied Moses and the seventy elders on Mount Sinai (Exod 24:1, 9) and had witnessed the great theophany (appearance of God) there. They died without male heirs (see also Exod 28:1; Num 3:2-4; 26:60-61; 1 Chr 6:3; 24:1-2). • The incense burners were fire pans or trays that held hot coals. Incense was sprinkled on them (Exod 30:34-38; see also Lev 16:12-13; 2 Chr 26:19; Rev 8:3-4). • The wrong kind of fire (Hebrew ’esh zarah, “strange fire”) could mean “foreign,” and thus “unauthorized” (see Exod 30:9) or even “pagan” (as in Ps 44:20; 81:9). Apparently, Nadab and Abihu used fire from a source not approved by God (Num 3:4; 26:61), possibly even a pagan source. It is also possible that they offered incense not prepared according to God’s specifications (Exod 30:34-38), although the text does not mention that. They did not enter God’s presence on his terms but on their own.

亞倫的兩個大兒子拿答和亞比戶（出6:23）曾和摩西及七十位長老一同上西奈山（出24:1、9），親眼看見神在那裡的顯現。他們死時沒有留下兒子（又見出28:1；民3:2-4；26:60-61；代上6:3；24:1-2）。

「香爐」是盛著燒紅火炭的火盆或托盤，香撒在火炭上（出30:34-38；又見利16:12-13；代下26:19；啟8:3-4）。

notes.en: Eleazar and Ithamar were Aaron’s two remaining sons (Exod 6:23). • leaving your hair uncombed: This practice and others like it were ways to show grief in biblical times (cp. Gen 37:29; 44:13; Deut 14:1; 2 Sam 1:11; Job 1:20; Jer 16:6; 47:5). As high priest, Aaron was prohibited from participating in these rituals or in any way displaying his grief (Lev 21:10). The injunction extended to Eleazar and Ithamar; if God’s representatives had shown grief on this occasion, it might have been interpreted by observers as disagreeing with God’s justice. However, the laypeople were allowed to mourn.

notes.en: These chapters detail the regulations pertaining to purity. The mixing of types of animals was forbidden (see Deut 22:9-11) because it represented a violation of the normal created order. “Abnormal” creatures—such as fish without fins and scales, carnivores, crawling insects, and animals without split hooves—cross boundaries between “normal” types and were unfit for food or offerings (see also Deut 14:1-21). The dietary laws were meant to distinguish Israel as a holy people from the surrounding nations (Lev 11:44-45).

notes.zh: 這幾章詳細說明有關潔淨的條例。不同種類的東西不可混雜（見申22:9-11），因為這違反了受造界原有的秩序。「不正常」的生物，例如沒有翅（鰭）和鱗的水族、吃肉的動物、爬行的昆蟲，以及不分蹄的走獸，都跨越了「正常」類別之間的界線，所以不適合作食物或祭物（又見申14:1-21）。飲食的條例是要使以色列成為聖潔的百姓，與周圍的列國分別出來（利11:44-45）。

notes.en: Some scholars have suggested that unclean animals were to be avoided for reasons of public health, but the evidence does not support this. Horse meat, for example, is no less healthy than beef, yet it was considered unclean because the horse does not have a split hoof (see 11:2-3). The regulations existed because an unclean animal was unacceptable as an offering to God and, therefore, it was also unacceptable as food for God’s people. Jesus proclaimed all foods clean for Christians (Mark 7:14-19; Acts 10:9-16).

notes.en: insects that walk along the ground and have jointed legs: This phrase eliminates creatures that creep or crawl low to the ground (11:27). Leviticus 11:42 indicates that multi-legged creatures, such as centipedes, are unclean. Locusts and grasshoppers are examples of clean insects (see Matt 3:4).

notes.zh: 「有足有腿，在地上蹦跳的」：這個說法排除了貼著地面爬行的生物（11:27）。11:42指出，像蜈蚣這樣多足的生物是不潔的。蝗蟲和蚱蜢是潔淨昆蟲的例子（見太3:4）。

notes.en: defiled until evening: Anyone who touched a carcass of an unclean animal would be unclean until evening, which marked the beginning of the next day in Israel.

notes.zh: 「必不潔淨到晚上」：凡摸了不潔動物屍體的人，都要不潔淨到晚上；在以色列，晚上是新的一天的開始。

notes.en: This list of unclean creatures that crawl contains both warm-blooded and cold-blooded animals that scurry along the ground. Snakes are also included in this category (11:42).

notes.zh: 這份不潔爬物的清單，包括在地上竄爬的溫血和冷血動物。蛇也屬於這一類（11:42）。

notes.en: Dead animals could make things and people unclean. Even a clean animal that died without having its blood drained was considered unclean (11:39-40). When a person became unclean from contact with an animal’s carcass, it lasted only until evening. Household articles that came into contact with a carcass had to be purified (11:25, 28, 32, 40) or destroyed (11:33, 35).

notes.en: A cistern was a hole dug into the ground or rock, often lined with plaster, that retained rain and surface water.

notes.zh: 「聚水的池子」是在地上或岩石中挖成的坑，內壁常抹上灰泥，用來儲存雨水和地面的水。

notes.en: Grain moistened with water was probably intended to be cooked for food; eating contaminated grain would be like eating a carcass. However, if the grain was sown, the new plant and the grain it bore were undefiled.

notes.en: Israelites were not to consume blood (7:26). They could eat an animal only after the blood had been drained and properly disposed of (17:13). The undrained blood of an otherwise clean animal that died of natural causes rendered it unclean. An Israelite was permitted to give or sell such an animal to foreigners (Deut 14:21) but not to eat it.

notes.en: I am the Lord your God: See study note on 18:2. • be holy, because I am holy: These words express the dominant theme of Leviticus: God is holy. He must be regarded and treated as holy, and he expects holiness from his people (10:3; 19:2). The profound teaching of this verse is that God’s own nature permeates those who covenant with him (see also 11:45; 20:7, 26; 21:8, 15; 22:9, 16, 32), and they become his holy people (Exod 22:31; Deut 28:9; cp. 1 Pet 1:16).

notes.zh:
「我是耶和華──你們的神」：見18:2的注釋。

「你們要成為聖潔，因為我是聖潔的」：這句話表達利未記最主要的主題：神是聖潔的。人必須以祂為聖、以聖潔待祂，而祂也期望祂的百姓聖潔（10:3；19:2）。這節經文深刻的教導是：神自己的本性要充滿那些與祂立約的人（又見11:45；20:7、26；21:8、15；22:9、16、32），使他們成為祂聖潔的子民（出22:31；申28:9；參彼前1:16）。

notes.en: brought you up from the land of Egypt: This or a similar phrase is found often throughout the Pentateuch (see 19:36; 22:33; 25:38; 26:13; Exod 13:9; 20:2; Num 15:41; Deut 4:37). Each time, it reminds the Israelites, God’s covenant people, of God’s great act in liberating them from Egypt. The Exodus event is frequently commemorated elsewhere in the Old Testament (Pss 80:8; 106:21; Isa 11:16; Jer 34:13; Hos 12:9; 13:4; Amos 2:10).

notes.zh: 「把你們從埃及地領出來」：這句話或類似的說法在摩西五經中常常出現（見19:36；22:33；25:38；26:13；出13:9；20:2；民15:41；申4:37）。每一次都提醒以色列這與神立約的子民，神曾施行大能把他們從埃及救出來。舊約其他地方也常常記念出埃及這件事（詩80:8；106:21；賽11:16；耶34:13；何12:9；13:4；摩2:10）。

notes.en: These verses detail the regulations pertaining to childbirth. Any bodily discharge, even blood, was considered “abnormal” because it reduced the vitality of the individual and rendered the person ceremonially unclean (see study notes on 5:3; 11:1–15:33). Accordingly, not childbirth but the discharge accompanying it is addressed in these verses (12:2, 5, 7). The uncleanness was not sinful in itself, but only if it was neglected and allowed to come into contact with what is holy (see 5:2-3).

notes.zh: 這幾節詳細說明有關生產的條例。身體流出的任何東西，甚至是血，都被視為「不正常」，因為它減損人的活力，使人在禮儀上不潔（見5:3；11:1–15:33的注釋）。因此，這幾節處理的不是生產本身，而是生產時流出的血（12:2、5、7）。不潔本身並不是罪；只有忽略不潔、讓它接觸到聖物時，才是罪（見5:2-3）。

notes.en: purification offering: The Hebrew word is the same as that for the sin offering (khatta’t, see study note on 4:1–5:13). This leads some scholars to think that this offering dealt only with purification or decontamination, including those cases mentioned in 5:1-6. The offering here was certainly part of a purification ritual, but it seems more likely that the sin offering repaired a lack or failure. In this context, the issue is purity rather than sin, and the focus is on restoring the woman to community fellowship, not forgiving a sinner.

notes.en: Concerning the regulations pertaining to infections, the principle of normal and abnormal comes into play (see “Clean, Unclean, and Holy” Theme Note). Whether in a person, clothing, or a building, infections are not normal: They indicate disease and death, the antitheses of wholeness, and were therefore declared unclean.

notes.zh: 在有關「災病」的條例中，「正常」與「不正常」的原則同樣適用。無論發生在人身上、衣服上或房屋上，災病都不正常：它們代表疾病和死亡，是完整的反面，所以被宣告為不潔。

notes.en: a serious skin disease (Hebrew tsara‘at): The Hebrew word is much broader than the severely disfiguring Hansen’s disease (see study note on 13:2). This larger range included symptoms such as an open sore (13:10), a boil (13:18), a burn (13:24), a sore on the head or chin (13:29), shiny white patches (13:38), or abnormal baldness (13:40). A general test was whether or not the abnormality was spreading (13:5-8). If so, a quarantine was ordered for as long as the disorder persisted (13:46). Not just people, but clothing (13:47-59) and even buildings (14:33-53) could contract such infections.

notes.zh: 「大痲瘋」（希伯來文 tsara‘at）：這個希伯來字所指的範圍，比會嚴重毀容的漢生病（俗稱痲瘋病）廣得多（見13:2的注釋）。它包括紅瘀肉（13:10）、瘡（13:18）、火毒（13:24）、頭上或鬍鬚上的災病（13:29）、白色的火斑（13:38）或不正常的禿頭（13:40）等症狀。一般的判斷標準是這不正常的狀況有沒有發散（13:5-8）。如果有，只要病還在，就要隔離（13:46）。不只是人，連衣服（13:47-59）甚至房屋（14:33-53）也會有這樣的災病。

notes.en: Skin disorders that were potentially contagious, such as swelling or a rash or discolored skin, required precautions to arrest their spread. Until a disorder was healed, the person was deemed unclean. The diseases described in this section may range from something as simple as an allergic rash, ringworm, or eczema to something as serious as gangrene. In Old Testament times, skin conditions were diagnosed by observation. The priests not only had a religious function, but they also served as physicians. • one of his sons: These priestly functions were to apply to future generations of priests as well.

notes.en: The Tabernacle containing the Ark was in the center of the camp so that God could be considered as being in the camp (Deut 23:14). As long as an individual’s skin disorder persisted, he or she was to stay in isolation . . . outside the camp. This ensured that the infection would not spread to others and that the uncleanness would not come in contact with holy things. Even Miriam, sister of Moses and Aaron, had to spend seven days outside the camp (Num 12:15). This area was not exclusive to those suffering from skin disorders. The uneaten sin offering was taken there and burned (Lev 4:21). Criminals were executed there (24:14, 23), and corpses were carried there to avoid contaminating the area where the people lived (10:4-5). Even bodily functions were attended to outside the camp (Deut 23:12-14).
notes.prepared: The Tabernacle containing the Ark was in the center of the camp so that God could be considered as being in the camp (申23:14). As long as an individual’s skin disorder persisted, he or she was to stay in isolation . . . outside the camp. This ensured that the infection would not spread to others and that the uncleanness would not come in contact with holy things. notes.zh: 存放約櫃的會幕位在營的中央，表示神就在營中（申23:14）。人的皮膚病只要還在，就要「獨居營外」。這樣可以確保病不會傳給別人，不潔也不會接觸到聖物。連摩西和亞倫的姊姊米利暗也必須在營外住七天（民12:15）。營外不只是給患皮膚病的人住的地方：不吃的贖罪祭要拿到那裡燒掉（利4:21），犯人在那裡被處死（24:14、23），屍體也抬到那裡，免得玷污百姓住的地方（10:4-5）。連人的便溺也要在營外處理（申23:12-14）。

notes.en: The rainy season in Israel, when the weather is humid and cool, extends from mid-October through March. Mildew flourishes during this time, and the spores can trigger serious allergic reactions, posing a health problem. The regulations for mildew in clothing were similar to those for infections in people. If the mildew showed signs of spreading, it was serious. If it could be stopped or washed or cut out, a garment could be saved. This process was also similar to the treatment of rot and mold in buildings (14:33-53).

Fresh water was also used in cleansing ceremonies (Num 8:7) and in sacrifice preparation (Lev 1:9, 13).

notes.zh: 「我若使……有大痲瘋的災病」：聖經的語言是絕對的一神觀，一切事都是神造成或容許的。例如出21:13把意外死亡描述為神容許發生的事（又見申19:4-5）。

notes.en: Having the house emptied indicated that it was not actually unclean until the priest pronounced it so. The owner would remove furnishings so that they would not be included in the quarantine.

notes.en: A summary statement about infections of all sorts (cp. 11:46-47).

notes.zh: 總結各種災病的條例（參11:46-47）。

notes.en: The principle of normal and abnormal and the created order again aids the interpretation of these regulations (see “Clean, Unclean, and Holy” Theme Note). Bodily discharges, such as infections (see study note on 13:1-46), were not “normal” because they weakened the vitality of the person, so the person was not seen as whole. Whether male (15:1-18) or female (15:19-33), such a person became unclean.

notes.zh: 「正常」與「不正常」以及受造秩序的原則，同樣有助於解釋這些條例。身體流出的東西，就像災病一樣（見13:1-46的注釋），並不「正常」，因為它減損人的活力，使人不被視為完整的。無論是男人（15:1-18）或女人（15:19-33），這樣的人都成為不潔。

notes.en: bodily discharge (literally a flowing from his flesh): Most scholars interpret the word flesh as a euphemism for sexual organs and the symptoms described here as indicating an infection of gonorrhea. Others suggest that it refers to a discharge of semen or even diarrhea. A discharge of semen is unlikely, however, because that is singled out in 15:16-17 and required only washing with water. It is clear that this bodily discharge proceeded from “under the man” (15:10) and contaminated anything he sat on or lay upon (15:4, 6, 9).

notes.zh: 「漏症」（原文是「從他肉體中流出來的」）：大多數學者認為，「肉體」是生殖器官的委婉說法，這裡描述的症狀表示是淋病之類的感染。也有人認為是指遺精，甚至是腹瀉。不過不太可能是遺精，因為遺精在15:16-17另外提到，而且只需要用水洗。很明顯，這漏症是從人的「身下」流出來的（15:10），會沾染他所坐或所躺的任何東西（15:4、6、9）。

notes.en: In contrast to the man with a skin disease (see 13:46), a man with a bodily discharge was apparently allowed to live at home. He did not have to undergo the more elaborate cleansing ritual described in ch 14. He simply had to wait seven days after the discharge ceased, wash (15:13), and present the least expensive animal sacrifice of two birds—one as a sin offering and the other as a whole burnt offering.

notes.en: In the case of an emission of semen, the discharge was not a sign of illness (see study note on 15:1-33). Still, the same rule applied; the man must wash and be considered unclean until the next evening.

notes.en: If the seminal emission involved sexual intercourse, both the man and the woman became unclean and had to wash and remain unclean until the next evening. Although it involved a bodily emission, sexual intercourse was not an infection or abnormality, and it required no sacrifices.

notes.zh: 若是在夫妻同房時遺精，男女兩人都成為不潔，必須洗澡，並且不潔淨到晚上。同房雖然牽涉到身體流出的東西，卻不是感染或不正常的情況，不需要獻祭。

notes.en: There is nothing wrong or diseased about a woman’s menstrual period. However, because it is accompanied by a bloody discharge, the woman was considered ceremonially unclean (see 15:32-33). The restrictions were similar to the restrictions on the man with the bodily discharge (15:2-12): She was allowed to live at home, but whatever she sat on became unclean. Anyone who touched her had to wash, and presumably she also did so at the end of the seven-day quarantine. However, no animal sacrifice was required.

notes.zh: 女人的月經沒有任何不對，也不是疾病。不過，因為伴隨著流血，女人在禮儀上被視為不潔（見15:32-33）。這些限制和對患漏症之男人的限制類似（15:2-12）：她可以住在家裡，但她所坐的東西都成為不潔。凡摸她的人都要洗澡；她自己大概也要在七天期滿時洗澡。不過，不需要獻上祭牲。

notes.en: Sexual intercourse with a woman during her menstrual period will later be forbidden and given a harsh penalty (18:19). This verse probably describes a case in which the woman’s menstrual flow went unnoticed when the sexual activity began or in which the woman’s period began during intercourse. The regulations required the man who came into contact with her blood to share the woman’s seven-day quarantine.

notes.en: Normal menstruation required no offering from the woman (15:19-24). A discharge of blood that exceeded seven days required a cleansing ceremony similar to that for the man cleansed of a bodily discharge (15:13-15; see also Matt 9:20-22).

notes.en: A summary of the principles stated in 15:1-31. Bodily discharges—whether pus, semen, menstrual fluid, or blood—made an individual ceremonially unclean.

notes.en: The Day of Atonement, the tenth day of the seventh month (see 16:29; 23:27; Num 29:7), was the most solemn day of the year for Israelites. It was the only required fast, and it was a Sabbath of rest for all the people (Lev 23:32). Introduced by the Festival of Trumpets (Num 29:1, 7-11), it was the day when the corporate sins of the community were atoned for. Only the high priest (Aaron) could officiate, because only he could represent all the people, including other priests (Aaron’s sons). The Day of Atonement is celebrated today as Yom Kippur.

It was the only required fast, and it was a Sabbath of rest for all the people (利23:32). Only the high priest (Aaron) could officiate, because only he could represent all the people, including other priests (Aaron’s sons). The Day of Atonement is celebrated today as Yom Kippur.
notes.zh: 贖罪日在七月初十（見16:29；23:27；民29:7），是以色列人一年中最莊嚴的日子。這是唯一規定要禁食的日子，也是全體百姓的安息聖日（利23:32）。贖罪日之前有吹角的節期（民29:1、7-11）。這一天要為整個群體的罪贖罪，只有大祭司（亞倫）可以主持，因為只有他能代表全體百姓，包括其他的祭司（亞倫的兒子們）。今天猶太人仍守這個節日，稱為 Yom Kippur。

notes.en: An inner curtain separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place. Conceptually, the sanctuary was God’s palace, the Most Holy Place was his throne room, and the Ark was his throne (see 1:1). In the ancient Near East, entering the presence of a king without invitation meant risking death (Esth 4:11). The Most Holy Place, therefore, was not a place that Aaron could enter casually. It was off-limits even to the high priest, except when his presence was required by God as part of the ritual of the Day of Atonement.

notes.zh: 內層的幔子把聖所和至聖所隔開。從觀念上來說，聖所是神的宮殿，至聖所是祂的寶座室，約櫃是祂的寶座（見1:1）。在古代近東，沒有受邀就進到君王面前，就要冒喪命的危險（斯4:11）。所以亞倫不可「隨時」進入至聖所。至聖所連大祭司也不可進入，只有在贖罪日的儀式中，神要求他進去時才可以。

notes.en: For most of the ritual of the Day of Atonement, the high priest wore plain linen clothing rather than his normal robes. This seems to symbolize the humility that should characterize all the people on this solemn occasion. When the high priest stood before God on behalf of his people, he had nothing to commend himself or the people. But when he stood before the people on God’s behalf, his official robes reflected the glory and splendor of God (16:23).

But when he stood before the people on God’s behalf, his official robes reflected the glory and splendor of God (16:23).
notes.zh: 贖罪日的儀式大部分時候，大祭司不穿平常的禮服，而是穿樸素的細麻布衣服。這似乎象徵在這莊嚴的日子，全體百姓都當存謙卑的心。大祭司代表百姓站在神面前時，他自己和百姓都沒有什麼可以誇口的；但他代表神站在百姓面前時，他的禮服就反映出神的榮耀和華美（16:23）。

notes.en: The writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews makes a clear analogy between Aaron’s work for Israel and Christ’s work for the believer. Both brought atonement to their people. Before Aaron could offer a sin offering for the people, he had to offer a sacrifice for himself to make certain his own sins were forgiven (Heb 5:1-3). However, although Christ was tempted, he did not sin (Heb 4:15). Therefore, in his role as high priest for all Christians, he had no need to make a similar sacrifice (Heb 7:26-28).

notes.zh: 希伯來書的作者把亞倫為以色列所做的，和基督為信徒所做的清楚地對照起來：兩者都為自己的百姓帶來贖罪。亞倫要為百姓獻贖罪祭之前，必須先為自己獻祭，確保自己的罪蒙了赦免（來5:1-3）。然而，基督雖然受過試探，卻沒有犯罪（來4:15）。所以祂作所有基督徒的大祭司，不需要為自己獻這樣的祭（來7:26-28）。

notes.en: The Hebrew term ‘aza’zel (Azazel) is found only in 16:8, 10, 26. This word has generally been interpreted in four different ways: (1) as a word meaning “the goat of going away”; (2) as a demon that lived in the wilderness; (3) as a strengthened form of the Hebrew word for “go, leave,” meaning “utter loss”; and (4) as a rocky cliff over which the goat was pushed. Since this goat represented the removal of the sins of Israel from the camp (16:22), the first interpretation is probably the simplest solution.

notes.zh: 希伯來字 ‘aza’zel（阿撒瀉勒）只出現在16:8、10、26。一般對這個字有四種解釋：（1）意思是「離去的山羊」；（2）住在曠野的一個鬼魔；（3）希伯來文「離開」一詞的加強形式，意思是「完全消失」；（4）一處山崖，山羊被推下崖去。既然這隻山羊代表把以色列的罪從營中除去（16:22），第一種解釋可能是最簡單的答案。

notes.en: The high priest needed to purify the Most Holy Place and the rest of the Tabernacle because, over the course of the year, the sins the Israelites had committed had brought uncleanness on the whole sanctuary. If the Tabernacle was to remain the place for meeting God in the coming year, it had to be purified. The same applied to the altar (16:18).

notes.en: For this ceremony, the high priest had to put on special clothing (16:4), which he used for no other purpose. When the ceremony concluded, he was to leave the garments in the Most Holy Place. Many scholars believe that the bathing and changes of clothing were necessary because handling the sin offering brought defilement.

notes.en: must deny yourselves: The Hebrew term (‘anah, “humble, afflict yourselves”) is closely connected with fasting (Isa 58:3, 5). • foreigners (Hebrew ger): The Hebrew term denotes those who were not Israelites yet lived among the Israelites. Foreigners participated to some extent in Israelite worship (see Num 9:14) and represented potential converts. They probably did not own land but were day laborers, share-croppers, or tenant farmers. However, if they lived among the Israelites, they were expected to abide by Israelite law and customs (see, e.g., Lev 24:16).

「寄居在你們中間的外人」（希伯來文 ger）：指不是以色列人、卻住在以色列人中間的人。他們在某種程度上參與以色列的敬拜（見民9:14），也是可能歸信的人。他們大概沒有自己的土地，而是作散工、佃農或租地耕種的人。不過，他們既住在以色列人中間，就要遵守以色列的律法和習俗（例如利24:16）。

notes.en: This section deals with how the community of Israel was to observe holiness. Holiness does not describe one attribute of God among many. Rather, it is the sum of all attributes of his person, nature, and character (see study note on Exod 3:5). His “glory” is the manifestation of his perfect person, nature, and character (see Lev 9:6). God’s covenant with Israel meant that the people and the nation participated in God’s holiness. This holiness depended on Israel’s relationship with God. This relationship brought certain ethical and ritual expectations for Israel to uphold.

notes.zh: 這一大段講論以色列群體當如何活出聖潔。聖潔不是神眾多屬性中的一項，而是祂位格、本性和品格一切屬性的總和（見出3:5的注釋）。祂的「榮耀」是祂完美的位格、本性和品格的彰顯（見利9:6）。神與以色列立約，表示這百姓和這國家都有分於神的聖潔。這聖潔取決於以色列與神的關係，而這關係為以色列帶來某些必須遵守的倫理和禮儀上的要求。

notes.en: These regulations (see also Deut 12:15-21) indicate that unsupervised sacrifice could easily lead to the integration of pagan elements into the true worship of the Lord (Lev 17:7). Israel was camped around the Tabernacle (Num 2:2-34), so it was not inconvenient to bring an animal to the sanctuary for slaughter. Deuteronomy 12:20-24 anticipates Israel’s settlement in the land and the hardship imposed by this regulation. It permitted slaughtering and eating meat without bringing it to the sanctuary, as long as the blood was not consumed.

notes.zh:
「流血的罪必歸到那人身上」：這人用不合法的方式流了牲畜的血。牲畜的生命是神所賜的，必須藉著祭牲的血歸還給神。

「從民中剪除」：見7:20-21的注釋。

notes.en: be unfaithful (Hebrew zanah, “commit fornication”): Israel was not to worship any god but the Lord (Exod 20:3). Israel’s covenant relationship to the Lord was even compared to a marriage (see Hos 1:2), and worshiping other gods could be described as spiritual adultery. In addition, many of the Canaanite religions were fertility cults. This verb reflects the prostitution conducted at Canaanite shrines to induce fertility in the land through rites of magic involving sexual intercourse. • The Hebrew word translated goat idols is the plural for a male goat. In the ancient world, the male goat was often a symbol of fertility or of a god of the underworld. During the reign of Jeroboam I, many Levites from the northern kingdom moved south to Jerusalem; they had been appalled by the use of goats and bulls in the northern kingdom’s worship (2 Chr 11:15-16).

notes.zh:
「行邪淫」（希伯來文 zanah，「行淫」）：以色列除了耶和華以外，不可敬拜別神（出20:3）。以色列與耶和華的立約關係甚至被比作婚姻（見何1:2），敬拜別神就是屬靈的淫亂。此外，許多迦南宗教是生殖崇拜，這個動詞也反映出迦南神廟中的廟妓，藉著與性有關的法術儀式，求使土地豐收。

譯作「鬼魔」的希伯來字是公山羊的複數。在古代世界，公山羊常是生殖力或陰間神明的象徵。耶羅波安一世作王時，北國有許多利未人南遷到耶路撒冷，因為他們對北國用山羊和牛犢的敬拜感到震驚（代下11:15-16）。

notes.en: the life of the body is in its blood: Israel was forbidden to consume blood (17:10) because it was symbolic of the life given by God and was reserved as God’s portion of each animal offering. God had also designated the sacrificial blood as the means of atonement. In other words, God’s grace permitted the life of the animal to be accepted in exchange for the life of the sinner. In the New Testament, the blood of Christ—representing his life freely given—has provided eternal redemption for believers (Heb 9:12).

notes.zh: 「活物的生命是在血中」：以色列人不可吃血（17:10），因為血象徵神所賜的生命，是每一份牲畜祭物中保留給神的部分。神也指定祭牲的血作為贖罪的方法。換句話說，神的恩典容許牲畜的生命被接納，代替罪人的生命。在新約中，基督的血代表祂甘心捨去的生命，為信徒成就了永遠贖罪的事（來9:12）。

notes.en: cover it with earth: This restriction kept the hunter from using an animal’s blood for food. Just like the blood of animals presented in altar offerings, the blood of wild game also represented life. Uncovered blood was also the sign of violent crime; innocent blood defiled the land (Num 35:33) and cried out to God for justice (Gen 4:10; see Job 16:18). Covering the blood of a slain animal gave it a symbolic burial. This demonstrated reverence both for the animal’s life and for God, the life-giver. The burial signified the return of that life to God, just like the disposal of the blood by the priest in the altar offerings.

notes.zh: 「用土掩蓋」：這個限制使打獵的人不能把獵物的血當食物。野生禽獸的血就像壇上祭牲的血一樣，也代表生命。沒有掩蓋的血也是暴力犯罪的記號：無辜人的血玷污了地（民35:33），並且向神呼求伸冤（創4:10；見伯16:18）。掩蓋被殺之動物的血，等於象徵性地埋葬牠，表示對牠的生命和賜生命的神都存敬畏的心。這樣的埋葬表示那生命歸回給神，正如祭司在壇上處理祭牲的血一樣。

notes.en: An animal killed by a predator or which died of natural causes still had undrained blood in its tissues. This rendered it ceremonially unclean and a potential source of defilement (22:8). Israelites were to throw such an animal to the dogs (Exod 22:31) or give or sell it to a non-Israelite (Deut 14:21). If an Israelite happened to eat an animal with undrained blood, he or she became ceremonially unclean and had to wash in water. The uncleanness itself was not a sin, but neglect of the unclean state brought punishment.

notes.en: Chapters 18 and 20 primarily discuss sexual matters, warning against engaging in pagan practices both religious and secular. These chapters bracket exhortations to pursue holiness in everyday life (ch 19).

notes.zh: 第18章和第20章主要討論性方面的事，警告人不可沾染異教在宗教和日常生活中的種種做法。這兩章包住了第19章，就是勸勉人在日常生活中追求聖潔的一章。

notes.en: Many Near Eastern treaties began with the name and titles of the ruler who was drawing up the treaty. The phrase I am the Lord your God gives the name of the Great King, Yahweh (English the Lord), followed by his title, your God (see also Exod 20:2; Deut 5:6). These words were an abbreviated way to invoke Israel’s covenant with God and all that it implied. By reminding the people that they were the Lord’s, these words carried an authority that required a response (Lev 11:44; 18:4-5). Chapter 18 begins and ends (18:30) with these words, and they appear frequently throughout chs 19–26.

notes.zh: 許多古代近東的條約，開頭都寫上訂約君王的名字和頭銜。「我是耶和華──你們的神」先說出大君王的名字雅威（中文聖經譯作「耶和華」），接著是祂的頭銜「你們的神」（又見出20:2；申5:6）。這句話是援引以色列與神所立的約及其一切含意的簡短說法。它提醒百姓他們是屬耶和華的，因此帶著要求回應的權柄（利11:44；18:4-5）。第18章以這句話開始，也以這句話結束（18:30），在19–26章中也常常出現。

notes.en: regulations . . . decrees: The Bible anticipated that the courts would need to interpret the laws that God had provided to apply them to different circumstances. Such interpretations became case laws; the body of these court decisions was called mishpatim in Hebrew (cp. “decrees” in 10:11). • Paul alludes to these verses in Rom 10:5 and Gal 3:12, where he contrasts the “way of faith” with the “way of law.”

notes.en: violate your father: The Hebrew text here equates having sexual relations with your mother or any of your father’s wives with having sexual relations with him (cp. Gen 35:22; 49:4; see also 1 Cor 5:1). The husband and his wife were “two united into one” (Gen 2:24; cp. Eph 5:29). Always in the background of these commands are the commands to honor your parents (Lev 20:9; Exod 20:12) and, by extension, other members of the family (see also study note on Lev 20:17).

notes.zh: 「羞辱了你父親」：希伯來原文把與自己的母親或父親的任何妻子發生性關係，等同於與父親發生性關係（參創35:22；49:4；又見林前5:1）。夫妻兩人「成為一體」（創2:24；參弗5:29）。這些命令的背後，始終有「孝敬父母」的命令（利20:9；出20:12），並延伸到家中其他的成員（又見利20:17的注釋）。

notes.en: She is your mother: Incest was prohibited because of the disruption it created in families, so the commands concerning this sin included close relatives not necessarily related by blood. Incest was a serious crime because it brought competition and chaos into the family structure. It threatened the safety of the home by violating a family’s appropriate intimacy and the sense of belonging shared by its members. • The commands were directly addressed to the male, even though the female could be older (such as one’s mother). The male, especially if he was the head of the household or the firstborn, wielded more power than the female; with this position came the responsibility to use that power lawfully. In addition, the male was more likely to be the sexual aggressor in an illicit sexual union, although this was not always the case (e.g., Gen 39:6-18).

這些命令是直接對男人說的，雖然女方可能比他年長（例如母親）。男人，特別是一家之主或長子，掌握的權力比女人大，這地位也帶著合法使用權力的責任。此外，在不正當的性關係中，男人比較可能是主動的一方，雖然不一定總是如此（例如創39:6-18）。

notes.en: Sexual relations with a full sister dishonored both parents, and relations with a half sister dishonored one parent.

notes.en: your father’s sister . . . mother’s sister: These actions would dishonor your father or mother.

notes.en: Having sexual relations with your aunt would dishonor your uncle. In turn, this would also dishonor your father (see 20:20).

notes.zh: 與伯叔母發生性關係，會羞辱你的伯叔，進而也羞辱你的父親（見20:20）。

notes.en: Just as having sexual relations with your father’s wife would dishonor your father, having sexual relations with your daughter-in-law would dishonor your son. The law called for daughters-in-law to be treated like natural daughters (Exod 21:9; cp. Gen 38:1-30).

notes.zh: 正如與父親的妻子發生性關係會羞辱父親，與兒媳發生性關係也會羞辱兒子。律法要求人待兒媳像待親生女兒一樣（出21:9；參創38:1-30）。

notes.en: Sexual relations with your sister-in-law would be adulterous and disgrace your brother. The exception was the law of levirate marriage (see Deut 25:5-10), which called for a man to marry his brother’s widow in order to produce an heir who was considered the dead brother’s son.

notes.en: As with all examples listed in ch 18, marrying a woman together with her daughter or granddaughter was prohibited because of the disruption it would cause in the family order. It would violate the intimacy of the family group by forcing a wife to compete for her husband’s affections against a much younger woman. The penalty for this act was death by burning (20:14).

notes.en: The word rivals (Hebrew tsarah) vividly describes the relationship between Leah and Rachel (Gen 29:16–30:24) and Hannah and Peninnah (1 Sam 1:6); in both cases, the fellow wives were driven to bitter rivalry for their husband’s affections.

notes.en: The Hebrew word translated defile yourself could be more literally translated to become ceremonially unclean. • Sexual intercourse with a neighbor’s wife or any married woman defined adultery in the Old Testament. Breaking this law was punishable by death (Deut 22:22). Like incest, adultery threatened the integrity and security of the home and family. In this case, it violated the covenant of marriage and divided the adulterer’s affection between his spouse and his mistress.

譯作「玷污自己」的希伯來字，更直接的譯法是「在禮儀上成為不潔」。

在舊約中，與鄰舍的妻子或任何已婚的女人發生性關係，就是「姦淫」。犯這律法的要被處死（申22:22）。姦淫和亂倫一樣，威脅家和家庭的完整與安全；它破壞婚約，使姦夫的感情分給了配偶和情婦。

notes.en: Molech was the national god of the Ammonites (1 Kgs 11:7). This god was later worshiped by Israel during times of apostasy (2 Kgs 23:10; Jer 32:35). Molech probably appears in this list because Molech worship was associated with sexual sins; it seems to have included child sacrifice as well. • To bring shame on (literally blaspheme, profane) the name of your God meant using the name of the Lord as though it were not holy, such as in a false oath (Lev 19:12) or in the worship of a false god (Ezek 20:39).

「褻瀆你神的名」，就是使用耶和華的名，卻不以它為聖，例如起假誓（利19:12）或敬拜假神（結20:39）。

notes.en: In Gen 1:31, God pronounced all things good. This yielded a theology of the created order where good is defined by what God created and by the way he intended it to function. Part of this “good” was the creation of woman as man’s companion (Gen 2:22-24). Marriage forms a microcosm of the human race, which stands as the corporate bearer of God’s image. Sin, introduced by the Fall (Gen 3), disrupted the created order. Homosexuality is but one example of sinful violation of God’s order; it is tied to the rejection of God by fallen humanity (Rom 1:25-32). • The Hebrew word translated detestable (to‘ebah) indicates strong disapproval and disgust (Lev 20:13; see also 18:26-30).

在創1:31，神宣告祂所造的一切都甚好。由此產生一種受造秩序的神學：「好」是由神所創造的，以及祂所定意的運作方式來界定的。這「好」的一部分，就是創造女人作男人的伴侶（創2:22-24）。婚姻是人類的縮影，而人類作為一個整體承載著神的形像。始祖墮落（創3章）帶進了罪，打亂了受造的秩序。同性性行為只是以罪違反神所定秩序的一個例子；它與墮落的人類棄絕神有關（羅1:25-32）。

notes.en: do not harvest. . . . Leave them for the poor: Israel’s covenant with God included a social structure that created a leveling effect and resisted social divisions. Families were required to provide for family members who faced difficulties. Widows and orphans (Exod 22:22), the poor, and foreigners (Lev 19:10) were considered members of Israel’s extended family. The poor were not only given special consideration in the offering system (5:7-13), but positive steps were taken to make sure they had food to eat.

notes.en: A society that did not respect the property of others would quickly fall apart internally. To steal was prohibited (Exod 20:15), and those who would deceive or cheat were required to present a guilt offering (see Lev 6:2-7).

A hired man needed to receive his wages promptly so that he could feed his family (Deut 24:15); to withhold the wages of such a worker was to cheat him.

It includes foreigners (Lev 19:34; cp. Luke 10:30-37). Conversely, hate leads to a grudge that can bear violent fruit (see 1 Jn 2:10-11; 4:20).

notes.zh: 「異類」……「兩樣攙雜」：神創造了自然的秩序（創1:31；見利18:22），越過神所定的界線就違反了這秩序。禁止混雜的規定也是給以色列人的實物教材：他們不可與迦南人通婚。

notes.en: Betrothal in the biblical world was considered equivalent to marriage. Sexual relations with a betrothed or engaged woman who was not a slave merited death, the same punishment as for adultery (Deut 22:22; see Lev 18:20). However, the situation was less clear when the woman was a slave who might be unable to refuse. While slaves in Israel had considerably more rights than those in Mesopotamia or Egypt, they were still not free. Because a slave girl could not be punished, the man was also left unpunished. Still, he was guilty in God’s sight and had to sacrifice a ram for his sin.

notes.zh: 在聖經的世界，訂婚被視為等同婚姻。與已許配或訂婚、而且不是奴僕的女子發生性關係，要被處死，和姦淫的刑罰相同（申22:22；見利18:20）。但女子若是婢女，情況就不那麼清楚，因為她可能無法拒絕。以色列的奴僕雖然比美索不達米亞或埃及的奴僕享有多得多的權利，仍然不是自由的。既然婢女不受刑罰，那男人也不受刑罰。不過，他在神眼中仍然有罪，必須為他的罪獻一隻公綿羊。

notes.en: For the first three years, a newly planted fruit tree was only to be pruned and cultivated. This allowed all the strength to go back into the tree. In the fourth year, all of the fruit was considered the “first crop” and was given to God (see Exod 23:16). Only in the fifth year could the fruit be eaten.

notes.en: Do not trim: As discovered in Egyptian wall paintings, Canaanites carefully trimmed their hair and beards. The Israelites were not to imitate this practice so that they would not be influenced by Canaanite religion and ethics.

notes.en: cut your bodies: Cutting oneself was associated with Canaanite mourning practices (21:5; Deut 14:1). The word translated tattoo might refer to painting the body, a practice also associated with paganism.

notes.en: Sabbath days: The Hebrew word translated “Sabbath” (shabbath) is related to a verb which means simply “to cease,” implying rest from one’s labor. The Sabbath commemorated God’s resting on the seventh day after he had completed his work of creation (Gen 1:31; 2:1-3). It began at sundown on the sixth day. With the exodus from Egypt, the Sabbath gained covenantal significance (Exod 16:23-25; 31:13). Because only free people, not slaves, had a regular day of rest, the Sabbath became symbolic of Israel’s liberation from bondage in Egypt (see Deut 5:13-15). • The people were to show reverence (literally fear) because the sanctuary, like the Sabbath, was holy. They were not to enter it when they were unclean or bring anything unclean into it.

notes.en: dishonest standards: Merchants would sometimes use two different sets of weights, one heavy and one light (Deut 25:13-15), in order to cheat customers. The Bible makes it clear that this practice was abhorrent to God (Prov 11:1; 16:11; 20:10, 23; Mic 6:11).

notes.en: Because pagan worship affected ethics, the regulations for families follow immediately after those dealing with pagan religious practices. To some extent, the laws of this section replicate those of 18:6-30, which precede the section dealing with proper expressions of holiness (19:1-37). These were all related issues, as the proper worship of God led to proper conduct toward other people, while improper worship of God led to moral violations.

notes.en: The Hebrew word for dishonors means “to make light of, treat with contempt,” and is traditionally translated “curse,” in the sense of calling someone a vulgar or profane name. Parental authority was given by God, not chosen by the child (see Exod 20:12; Deut 21:18-21).
