notes.en: Being left childless carried a social stigma and was considered a judgment from God (see Gen 30:1-2; Deut 7:14). What situation is envisioned in these verses? Sexual relations with a sister-in-law (Lev 18:16) or an uncle’s wife (18:14) have already been discussed. Adultery is dealt with elsewhere and would bring death to both parties (Deut 22:22). If the woman involved was a widow without a male heir, the law of levirate marriage could be invoked (Deut 25:5-6; see study note on Lev 18:16). Since those situations don’t seem to apply, it would appear that this law refers to marrying an aunt or a sister-in-law after she has been divorced from her husband. John the Baptist apparently applied this law to condemn Herod Antipas’s marriage to Herodias (see Mark 6:17-29).

notes.en: The expression flowing with milk and honey is common in Exodus—Deuteronomy. It conveys the idea of food being abundant and easy to get. This contrasts with Egypt, where everything depended on the flooding of the Nile and irrigation (Deut 11:9-12).

notes.en: This section, which covers priestly regulations, is punctuated six times with the phrase I am the Lord who makes . . . holy (21:15, 23; 22:9, 16, 32; cp. 21:8). Priests are specifically addressed in 21:1–22:16, while both clergy and laity are included in 22:17-33.

excerpts.en: I am the Lord who makes . . . holy
excerpts.zh: 我是叫他們成聖的耶和華

notes.title: 21:1–22:33 總覽
notes.zh: 這一段講論祭司的條例，其中六次出現「我是叫他們成聖的耶和華」這類話（21:15、23；22:9、16、32；參21:8）。這些話再次肯定神的聖潔與祭司當有的聖潔之間必然的關聯，並延伸到全以色列（見8:10；11:44-45；19:2）。21:1–22:16專門對祭司說，22:17-33則同時包括祭司和一般百姓。

notes.en: Touching a dead body rendered a person unclean for seven days. Because a priest had to be prepared to deal with holy things at all times, he was not allowed to handle a dead body, even of a relative, or else he could be unfit to minister when needed. The only exceptions were his closest relatives because there might not be anyone else who could bury the bodies.

notes.zh: 摸了屍體的人要不潔淨七天。祭司必須隨時預備處理聖物，所以不可接觸屍體，即使是親屬的屍體也不可以，否則需要他供職的時候，他可能就不合用。唯一的例外是他最近的骨肉之親，因為可能沒有別人能埋葬他們。

notes.en: shave . . . trim: See study notes on 10:6; 19:27. • cut their bodies: See study note on 19:28. Self-mutilation was a pagan custom. Just as defects of any kind precluded most animals as offerings (22:19-25), a defect similarly precluded a priest from officiating (see 21:17-23). For example, a eunuch could not serve as a priest (Deut 23:1) because he was not an adequate representative of the people. However, his priestly lineage was recognized as qualifying him to eat his priestly share (see Lev 21:22). On the other hand, uncleanness disqualified any priest from ministry and from eating the priest’s share as long as the condition persisted (22:2-8).

「用刀劃身」：見19:28的注釋。自殘身體是異教的習俗。正如有任何殘疾的牲畜大多不能作祭物（22:19-25），祭司身上有殘疾也同樣不能供職（見21:17-23）。例如閹割的人不能作祭司（申23:1），因為他不足以代表百姓；不過他的祭司血統仍被承認，使他可以吃祭司的分（見利21:22）。另一方面，任何祭司只要處在不潔的狀態，就不能供職，也不能吃祭司的分（22:2-8）。

notes.en: A priest should never bring shame by profaning God’s name.

notes.zh: 祭司絕不可「褻瀆神的名」，使神的名蒙羞。

notes.en: The priest, to lead Israel in worship, had to model the highest standard of conduct for the people both in his personal life and in leadership of his family. He could have no ties to pagan culture (prostitution, 21:9), nor could the legitimacy of his family be questioned (divorce). Similar standards applied to leaders of the early church (1 Tim 3:1-13).

notes.en: The restrictions made on the common priests (21:1-4) applied even more stringently to the high priest because he had to represent all Israel, including the other priests. • The priest must never leave his hair uncombed or tear his clothing in mourning, so that he would always be fit to minister. Although the common priest was permitted to marry a widow, the high priest was allowed to marry only a virgin. This made certain that the future high priest and the common priests descended from that union would have an unquestioned lineage (21:15).

notes.zh:
對一般祭司的限制（21:1-4），用在大祭司身上更加嚴格，因為他必須代表全以色列，包括其他的祭司。

大祭司「不可蓬頭散髮，也不可撕裂衣服」表示哀悼，好讓他隨時都能供職。一般祭司可以娶寡婦，大祭司卻只能娶處女。這樣可以確保從這婚姻所生、將來作大祭司和一般祭司的後代，血統無可置疑（21:15）。

notes.en: he may eat: Although a mutilation or defect (see 21:18-20) disqualified a descendant of Aaron from representing the people, it did not compromise his priestly lineage. He was eligible to eat the priest’s share of the offerings (see 2:3, 10; 6:17-18).

notes.en: Passover began at sundown on the fourteenth day of the first month, as the new day was beginning (see study note on 11:24-25). The Passover feast included a roast lamb, bitter salad greens, and bread made without yeast (Exod 12:8), all representing Israel’s liberation from Egyptian bondage. • The first month marked the beginning of the Jewish calendar as late as Ezra 6:19. The month’s earliest name, Abib (“spring, fresh grain”; Exod 13:4; 23:15; 34:18; Deut 16:1), was partially replaced by the name Nisan after the Babylonian exile (Neh 2:1; Esth 3:7).

notes.en: Just as the burned portion of each sacrifice represented the whole offering and the tithe symbolized that all of a person’s money belonged to God, so also the first portions of each harvest, or first crops, symbolized the entire harvest, and even the land itself (25:23), as belonging to the Lord. In the barley harvest, the first portions were offered as part of the Festival of Unleavened Bread (23:6, 10-12). The first portions of the wheat harvest were offered during the Festival of Harvest (23:15-21; Exod 34:22). These gifts to God recognized God’s prior gifts to Israel (see Lev 2:1). The entire offering of first crops became the property and food of God’s representatives, the priests (see 2:14-16).

notes.zh: 每一份祭物中燒掉的部分代表整份祭物，十分之一象徵人所有的錢財都屬於神；同樣，每次收成的第一部分，就是「初熟的莊稼」，象徵全部的收成，甚至土地本身（25:23），都屬於耶和華。收割大麥時，初熟的部分要在無酵節中獻上（23:6、10-12）；收割小麥時，初熟的部分要在七七節獻上（23:15-21；出34:22）。這些獻給神的禮物，承認神先賜給了以色列（見利2:1）。初熟的供物全部歸給神的代表，就是祭司，作他們的財物和食物（見2:14-16）。

notes.en: Israel was to start the count of seven full weeks on the first day of the Festival of Unleavened Bread. The fiftieth day marked the beginning of the Festival of Harvest (the New Testament name of “Pentecost” is derived from the Greek word for “fifty”). For this festival the people were to offer the first portions of the wheat harvest. Each person was also required to take three quarts of fine flour and bake two loaves of yeast bread. These offerings were then presented to the priest officiating at the sanctuary. See also study note on Exod 23:16.

notes.en: On the first day of the appointed month in early autumn: The Israelite calendar was divided into two half-years. The first half-year began with the first month, Nisan (Babylonian name) or Abib (the more ancient agricultural name). The second half-year began with the seventh month (Tishri in the modern Jewish calendar). The celebration of this holiday marked the beginning of the second half-year.

notes.en: The Day of Atonement was the most solemn day in the Israelite calendar and the only day of fasting (ch 16). The high priest made atonement for the corporate sin of the people, laying the theological foundation for the atonement made by Jesus Christ (Heb 9:11-12).

notes.en: During the Festival of Shelters, the Israelites lived in temporary shelters for seven days. This commemorated the time they had spent in tents and other temporary shelters during the wilderness wanderings and also recalled God’s faithfulness to them during those times. For a list of sacrifices to be offered each day, see Num 29:12-34.

Their understanding of who they were and of who God was revolved around their knowledge of those things. See Deut 6:20-24; 26:5-9; Josh 24:2-13; Ps 136.

This bread was considered part of the priest’s portion of the offerings. David and his men ate this bread while fleeing from Saul (1 Sam 21:1-6; see Matt 12:1-8).

notes.en: A large body of non-Israelites, including other Semitic people as well as Egyptians, came out of Egypt with Israel (Exod 12:38). Among them was a man of mixed parentage, whose mother was an Israelite and whose father was an Egyptian. A quarrel broke out between the man and a full-blooded Israelite. In the altercation, the man who was half-Egyptian verbally cursed the Israelite, using the name of God in an irreverent manner.

notes.zh: 有一大群不是以色列人的人，包括其他閃族人和埃及人，跟著以色列人一同出了埃及（出12:38）。其中有一個混血的人，母親是以色列人，父親是埃及人。這人和一個純以色列血統的人起了爭執；爭吵中，這個有一半埃及血統的人出口咒詛那以色列人，並且不敬地使用神的名。

notes.en: blasphemed . . . with a curse In biblical times, a name was more than a means of identification; it represented a person’s character, reputation, and origin. God is holy, and he was to be regarded as holy in all of Israel’s life (see 10:3). The Israelites had been instructed to treat God’s name with reverence (Exod 20:7). Using his name in a curse reflected a sinful attitude toward God himself (Lev 24:15), and it deserved death (24:13-16). The wording in the Hebrew text is very strong: Two verbs meaning “curse” are used, one that indicated a more formal type of curse, the other a blasphemous or irreverent expression. The two terms are synonymous in 24:15-16. • the Name of the Lord: The Hebrew text refers simply to “the Name” to reflect care and reverence for God’s name.

notes.zh:
「褻瀆了聖名，並且咒詛」：在聖經時代，名字不只是辨識的方式，更代表一個人的品格、名聲和來歷。神是聖的，在以色列生活的一切事上都要以祂為聖（見10:3）。以色列人曾受吩咐要敬重神的名（出20:7）。用神的名咒詛人，反映出對神自己有罪的態度（利24:15），該當死罪（24:13-16）。希伯來原文的措辭非常強烈：用了兩個意思是「咒詛」的動詞，一個指較正式的咒詛，另一個指褻瀆或不敬的言語；這兩個字在24:15-16是同義的。

「聖名」：希伯來原文只說「那名」，表示對神的名的慎重和敬畏。

notes.en: Those who heard a blasphemer curse were to lay their hands on his head. This indicated their own innocence by symbolically transferring the guilt (see 16:21), as well as their willingness to accept responsibility for the blasphemer’s death. A single witness was not enough to cause a man to die (see Num 35:30; Deut 17:2-7; Matt 18:16; 2 Cor 13:1; 1 Tim 5:19; Heb 10:28).

notes.en: Because human life was patterned after the life of God himself (Gen 1:26, 27), murder was a blasphemous act. It required the same penalty as oral blasphemy (Gen 9:6). For a similar law and its qualifiers, see Exod 21:12-14.

notes.zh: 人的生命是照著神自己的形像造的（創1:26、27），所以殺人是褻瀆的行為，要受和口頭褻瀆相同的刑罰（創9:6）。類似的律法和它的限定條件，見出21:12-14。

notes.en: eye for an eye: The legal principle involved is often called lex talionis (“law of retaliation”), which is that the penalty must fit the crime. When an injured party sought revenge on behalf of their kinsman (see Num 35:19-21), excessive revenge naturally ensued instead of appropriate justice. This provoked even greater retaliation, resulting in a cycle of increasing violence. Lex talionis served to regulate the prosecution of crimes (see also Lev 6:2-7; cp. Exod 21:24; Lev 24:20; Deut 19:21; Matt 5:28-39).

notes.zh: 「以眼還眼」：這個法律原則常稱為「同態復仇法」（lex talionis），意思是刑罰必須和罪行相稱。受害的人為親屬報仇時（見民35:19-21），往往會過度報復，而不是施行適當的公義，結果引發更大的報復，使暴力不斷升高。同態復仇法的作用是規範對罪行的追究（又見利6:2-7；參出21:24；申19:21；太5:38-39）。

notes.en: Although foreigners were not citizens, they were human beings entitled to equal justice under the law (see 16:29, 31).

notes.zh: 外人雖然不是以色列的公民，卻也是人，在律法之下有權得到同樣的公義（見16:29、31）。

notes.en: Just as seven days equaled a week ending in a Sabbath day, each seven years ended with a Sabbath year. Likewise, after seven Sabbath years (i.e., 49 years total) came a special year, the Year of Jubilee. Like so many holidays, these occasions were times of reflection on Israel’s corporate identity and how they were shaped by their relationship with God. Because every Israelite, bond or free, had a part in God’s kingdom, those bound in servitude were freed in the Year of Jubilee (25:39-43). In order to curb economic hardship and foster well-being, land sales were limited to a maximum term of fifty years. The land was then to be returned to the original owner’s family or clan. The land belonged to the Lord; the Israelites were merely tenants (25:23). It is unlikely, however, that these laws saw much use; the best land fell into the hands of rich landowners (Isa 5:8-10; cp. Amos 5:11).

notes.zh: 七天為一週，最後一天是安息日；同樣，每七年的最後一年是安息年。過了七個安息年（共四十九年），又有一個特別的年，就是禧年。和許多節日一樣，這些日子是讓以色列反省自己作為一個群體的身分，以及他們如何被與神的關係所塑造。因為每個以色列人，無論為奴或自由，都在神的國中有分，所以在禧年，賣身為奴的人要得自由（25:39-43）。為了減輕經濟困境、促進安康，土地的買賣最長以五十年為限，期滿後要歸還原主的家族或宗族。地是屬耶和華的，以色列人只是寄居的（25:23）。不過，這些律法大概很少被實行；最好的土地落入了富有地主的手中（賽5:8-10；參摩5:11）。

notes.en: During the year of Sabbath rest, there was to be no formal cultivation or harvesting of the land; from what grew on its own the landowner could gather what he needed for his household day by day. Whatever remained uneaten was left for the poor and for foreigners (Exod 23:10-11), and what they left provided food for both wild and domestic animals. See also Exod 21:2; Deut 15:1-11.

notes.en: land must have a Sabbath year: The principle behind the Sabbath (see study note on 19:30) was that God rested and therefore man rests. Here the principle was extended to the land.

notes.zh: 「地要守聖安息」：安息日的原則（見19:30的注釋）是：神安息了，所以人也要安息。這裡把這原則延伸到土地上。

notes.en: The Year of Jubilee took place every fiftieth year as a release from obligations and servitude. The same year was also treated as a Sabbath year with no farming. Some scholars argue that the forty-ninth year served as both Sabbath (seventh) and jubilee (fiftieth) years. A simple count of fifty years would place the Year of Jubilee immediately after the seventh Sabbath year, which would mean two consecutive years without harvests. • Each Year of Jubilee the land was to revert to the clan or tribe that had originally received it under Joshua (Josh 13–21). Land had two functions: (1) It provided an economic basis for existence; and (2) it tied the landowner to his ancestors and, through them, to the land allocation under Joshua and even to the covenant with Moses. The return of the land was to prevent powerful land monopolies that would close out the poor.

notes.zh:
禧年每第五十年一次，是解除債務和奴役的一年，同時也當作安息年，不可耕種。有些學者認為，第四十九年同時是安息年（第七個）和禧年（第五十年），因為若單純數五十年，禧年就緊接在第七個安息年之後，等於連續兩年沒有收成。

每逢禧年，土地要歸還當年在約書亞時代分得這地的宗族或支派（書13–21章）。土地有兩個功能：（1）提供生存的經濟基礎；（2）把地主與他的祖先連結起來，並藉著祖先連結到約書亞時代的分地，甚至連結到摩西所立的約。歸還土地是為了防止強大的土地壟斷，把窮人排除在外。

notes.en: proclaim freedom throughout the land for all who live there: See 25:39-43, 47-55. • return to the land that belonged to your ancestors: If the individual who originally owned the land had died, the land was returned to his heirs.

notes.en: the number of years: The law did not allow the land to be sold in perpetuity. It was God’s, and Israel was simply permitted to use it (25:23). However, if the owner was forced to give it up due to financial distress, it could be leased for up to forty-nine years (until the next jubilee). The price was adjusted according to the length of the lease. At the end of that time, the land was to revert to the family of the original owner.

notes.zh: 「按……年數」：律法不容許土地被永久賣斷。地是神的，以色列只是獲准使用（25:23）。不過，地主若因經濟困難被迫放棄土地，可以把地租出去，最長四十九年（到下一個禧年為止），價錢按租期長短調整。期滿後，土地要歸還原主的家族。

notes.en: the land belongs to me: Israel’s ownership of the land was derivative, not absolute—ownership depended on the covenant, in which God himself allotted them the land (Deut 1:8, 39). The ideas of land stewardship and of sharing material resources stem naturally from this concept of God’s ownership.

notes.zh: 「地是我的」：以色列對土地的擁有權是衍生的，不是絕對的；這擁有權取決於約，是神自己把地分給他們的（申1:8、39）。管家職分以及分享物質資源的觀念，很自然地從「神擁有一切」這個觀念而來。

notes.en: The Hebrew word translated buy it back (ga’al) is often translated “redeem.” It means “to restore something to its original or proper state of existence.” The noun derived from this root (go’el) indicates the close relative who will restore what is out of order. The relative’s duties were to redeem the property of his kinsman and keep it in the family (see Ruth 4:1-4; Jer 32:6-15); to seek out the murderer of his kinsman and bring him to justice (Num 35:19); and to marry his brother’s widow and father a male heir to inherit the estate of his dead kinsman (Deut 25:5-10; see Gen 38:6-30; Ruth 4:9-10).

notes.zh: 譯作「贖回」的希伯來字（ga’al）意思是「使某物恢復原本或應有的狀態」。由這個字根而來的名詞（go’el）是指要把失序之事恢復過來的近親。這近親的責任包括：贖回親屬的產業，使它留在家族中（見得4:1-4；耶32:6-15）；追查殺害親屬的人，使他伏法（民35:19）；娶弟兄的遺孀，為死去的親屬生子繼承產業（申25:5-10；見創38:6-30；得4:9-10）。

notes.en: A house in an unwalled village was apparently considered the same as land. It could be bought back, and if not, ownership reverted in the Year of Jubilee to the family of the individual who sold it. No farm or grazing acreage was involved in the sale of a house inside a walled town. Because such a house could be built on the town wall without having to rest on the earth (Josh 2:15), there was no land to redeem. Therefore, it could not be bought back unless the new owner desired to sell it, nor did it revert to the original owner in the Year of Jubilee.

notes.zh: 無城牆村莊裡的房屋，看來被視為和田地一樣：可以贖回，若沒有贖回，到禧年就歸還賣主的家族。城內的住宅則不牽涉耕地或牧地；這樣的房屋可以建在城牆上，不必建在地上（書2:15），所以沒有土地可贖。因此除非新屋主願意賣，否則不能贖回，到禧年也不歸還原主。

notes.en: The tribe of Levi could not inherit tribal territory because, as the priestly tribe, they were scattered throughout the land (Deut 18:1; see Gen 49:5-7; Num 35:1-8; Josh 21:1-42). The Levites could inherit only certain cities and the pasturelands surrounding them (Num 35:2). Therefore, they were an exception to the rules regarding land ownership, and their meager holdings were carefully protected. Their houses could be redeemed even in walled cities, and the pasturelands outside their towns could not be sold.

notes.en: Impoverished Israelites first looked to family for help (see study note on 25:25). Second, they relied on the community, which was commanded to help them rather than exploit their vulnerability.

notes.en: As human beings created in God’s image (Gen 1:26, 27; Prov 14:31; 17:5) and as fellow Israelites in covenant with God, even bondservants were to be treated with respect. God’s law includes numerous provisions for their protection (see Exod 21:20, 26-27). All human beings must be treated in a way that reflects reverence for God (see Prov 14:31; 17:5; Jas 2:14-16; 3:9-10).

notes.zh: 人是照神的形像造的（創1:26、27；箴14:31；17:5），奴僕又是與神立約的以色列同胞，所以也要受尊重。神的律法有許多保護他們的條文（見出21:20、26-27）。對待一切的人，都要顯出對神的敬畏（見箴14:31；17:5；雅2:14-16；3:9-10）。

notes.en: Slaves in Mesopotamia and Egypt were little more than chattel, with no protection or rights. Israelites were allowed to purchase non-Israelites as slaves, but they were to be treated well and not abused. Occasionally some slaves were even adopted into childless families (Gen 15:2-4). Slavery continued into New Testament times, but the foundations had been laid for its dissolution in the Old Testament doctrine of the common origins of all humankind through God. Slavery stemmed from the Fall, when relationships based on power replaced those of fellowship and communication (see Gen 3:16). In the New Testament, believers uphold the ideas of fellowship and communication by accepting the title “Christ’s slave” or “servant” (Rom 1:1; Col 4:12; 2 Pet 1:1). In Paul’s doctrine of the body of Christ (1 Cor 12:27; Eph 4:12), all believers acquired a common identity (Gal 3:28; Col 3:11; Phlm 1:16).

notes.zh: 在美索不達米亞和埃及，奴隸幾乎只是財產，沒有任何保障或權利。以色列人可以買非以色列人作奴僕，但要善待他們，不可虐待；有時甚至有奴僕被沒有兒女的家庭收養（創15:2-4）。奴隸制度一直延續到新約時代，但舊約「全人類都源自神」的教導，已經為廢除奴隸制度打下了根基。奴役源自人的墮落，那時以權力為基礎的關係取代了相交和溝通（見創3:16）。在新約中，信徒接受「基督的僕人」這個稱號（羅1:1；西4:12；彼後1:1），持守相交與溝通的理想。在保羅「基督的身體」的教導中（林前12:27；弗4:12），所有信徒都有了共同的身分（加3:28；西3:11；門1:16）。

notes.en: An Israelite who sold himself or a family member to a foreigner in Israel retained the right to buy himself or the family member back. If he could not find the resources to do that, he was not released during the seventh year (cp. Exod 21:2) but had to await the Year of Jubilee. During his service to the foreigner, the Israelite slave was to enjoy the status of a hired servant and not be treated like a slave (Lev 25:53). The people of Israel belonged to God; they were not to be sold as permanent slaves to anyone else.

notes.zh: 以色列人若把自己或家人賣給住在以色列的外人，仍保有贖回自己或家人的權利。如果他籌不到錢，第七年也不得釋放（參出21:2），要等到禧年。他服事外人的期間，要享有雇工人的地位，不可被當作奴僕看待（利25:53）。以色列百姓屬於神，不可被賣給任何人作永久的奴僕。

notes.en: Israel was to make no idols or carved images to worship (see Exod 20:4-6). Creating an image to worship would blaspheme God by confining him to time and space and by manufacturing a lifeless image to take the place of the living God. • Early in Israel’s history, stones were set on end as memorials to various events (Gen 28:18; Exod 24:4). However, pillars and sculptured stones were associated with pagan worship (2 Kgs 3:2; 10:26, 27), especially when the carved image of a god rested on them. Some sculpture was clearly allowed (e.g., 1 Kgs 7:25); the focus here is on objects that might be worshiped and thereby become idolatrous.

notes.zh:
以色列不可製作偶像或雕刻的像來敬拜（見出20:4-6）。造像來敬拜，等於把神限制在時空之中，又用沒有生命的像取代永活的神，是褻瀆神的。

在以色列歷史的早期，人會立起石頭來記念某些事件（創28:18；出24:4）。然而柱像和鏨成的石像與異教的敬拜有關（王下3:2；10:26、27），特別是上面放著神像的時候。有些雕刻是明顯被容許的（例如王上7:25）；這裡的重點是可能被人敬拜、因而成為偶像的東西。

notes.en: These blessings and curses resemble a key element of ancient Near Eastern suzerain-vassal treaties. In such treaties, the suzerain king promised to defend the vassal king and his state, while the vassal took an oath of loyalty to his lord. Blessings and curses followed, with the curses generally being more lengthy (contrast 26:3-13 with 26:14-39; cp. Deut 27:15–28:68). Such treaties would call upon the gods as witnesses and enforcers. In God’s covenant with Israel, however, the Lord was one of the parties to the treaty (Israel being the other); since the Lord could swear by no one greater, he swore by himself (see Gen 22:16; Heb 6:13).

notes.en: Treaties and covenants had conditions attached to them. Israel’s blessings were conditioned on the people’s obedience to the terms revealed by God, to whom they had sworn obedience (Exod 24:7; Josh 24:21-22). The covenant itself, however, was irrevocable (Lev 26:44-45; see Rom 11:29); Israel could not cancel it. The people had only two choices: obedience, which brought blessing, or rebellion, which brought curse.

notes.en: Israel’s restoration following captivity also promised a harvest so plentiful that it would run over into the time of planting (see Amos 9:13; Joel 3:18).

notes.zh: 以色列被擄歸回後的復興，也應許莊稼豐收到延續到撒種的時候（見摩9:13；珥3:18）。

notes.en: Success in warfare would result from obedience to God (cp. 26:17, 36-37; Deut 28:6, 19).

notes.en: fulfill my covenant: The fulfillment is seen in the “rest” spoken of in Hebrews (Heb 3:11–4:11). The Promised Land should have brought a state of security and prosperity, a state of “rest” to the Israelites (Exod 33:14; Deut 12:10; 25:19; Josh 1:13, 15). Israel succeeded in entering the Promised Land, but their rebellion kept them from seeing the covenant fulfilled.

notes.en: your God . . . my people: The covenant bound the parties to one another, making each belong to the other.

excerpts.zh: 作你們的神……作我的子民

notes.zh: 「作你們的神……作我的子民」：這約使立約的雙方彼此委身、互相歸屬。

notes.en: yoke of slavery: A yoke would fit over a slave’s shoulders and behind the base of the neck for carrying pairs of heavy items, such as pails of water. Cp. Rom 6:16-22.

notes.zh: 「軛」：奴僕把軛架在肩上、頸後，用來挑兩件重物，例如兩桶水。參羅6:16-22。

notes.en: The objective of God’s punishment of his people is to change behavior and restore relationship. God responds to his disobedient people as a perfectly righteous and loving parent would to a child. The punishments designed to curb rebellious behavior gradually increase, giving Israel the opportunity to repent at any time (26:18-28). Even when Israel was punished with exile from the land in 722 and 586 BC, God was working to restore his people (see, e.g., Isa 40–66; Jer 29:10; Amos 9:11-15).

notes.en: seven times over: I.e., many times (see also 26:21, 24, 28; Gen 4:15).

notes.en: If God withholds rain, the ground will be hard and unproductive.

notes.zh: 神若不降雨，地就會堅硬如銅，不出土產。

notes.en: Starvation would so pervade the land that when a child died of hunger, he or she would be eaten, in pagan fashion, by the others in the family (Deut 28:53-57; see 2 Kgs 6:24-31; Lam 2:20; cp. 2 Kgs 3:27).

notes.en: The pagan shrines mentioned here were the infamous “high places” built on hilltops (see 2 Kgs 18:4). These shrines incorporated elements from pre-Israelite religions into Israel’s worship and challenged the Temple for religious authority. • places of worship (Hebrew khamman): Perhaps “incense altars.” Some of these altars were used in Baal worship (2 Chr 34:4).

這裡提到的「邱壇」就是惡名昭彰、建在山頂上的「高處」（見王下18:4）。這些地方把以色列人進入迦南以前就有的宗教成分摻進以色列的敬拜中，並且與聖殿爭奪宗教的權威。

「日像」（希伯來文 khamman）：可能是指「香壇」。有些這樣的壇用在巴力的敬拜中（代下34:4）。

notes.en: With the people gone into captivity in a foreign land, there would be no one to work the land. It would at last have the “rest” of lying fallow that the people had denied it (see 25:1-7).

notes.zh: 百姓被擄到外邦之地，就沒有人耕種這地。這地終於能休耕，享受百姓一直不給它的「安息」（見25:1-7）。

notes.en: Disastrous defeat and captivity would later be the fate of both Israel and Judah (see study notes on 18:28; 26:14-39).

notes.zh: 後來以色列和猶大都遭遇了慘敗和被擄的命運（見18:28；26:14-39的注釋）。

notes.en: The chapter ends with a message of hope: Even after Israel violated the covenant and experienced judgment, reconciliation and restoration remained possible if the people confessed and repented (see study note on 4:20). God’s grace had not been taken away. God did not want to destroy his people; he would restore them if they would only humble themselves and repent (see also 2 Chr 7:14).

notes.zh: 這一章以盼望的信息作結：即使以色列違背了約、經歷了審判，只要百姓承認罪過、悔改，仍然可以與神和好、得著復興（見4:20的注釋）。神的恩典沒有被收回。神並不想毀滅祂的百姓；只要他們自卑悔改，祂就要恢復他們（又見代下7:14）。

notes.en: Physical circumcision of males was the mark of God’s covenant with Israel (Gen 17:9-14; Exod 4:25-26). Stubborn hearts (literally uncircumcised hearts) do not love God and demonstrate it by persistent disobedience. God promised to “circumcise” Israel’s uncircumcised hearts so that the people could love him (see also Deut 10:16; 30:6; Jer 4:4; Ezek 36:25-27).

notes.zh: 男人肉身受割禮是神與以色列立約的記號（創17:9-14；出4:25-26）。「未受割禮的心」不愛神，並以一再的悖逆顯明出來。神應許要給以色列「未受割禮的心」行割禮，使百姓能夠愛祂（又見申10:16；30:6；耶4:4；結36:25-27）。

notes.en: God had begun his covenant with Abraham (then called Abram, Gen 15:18) and continued it with Isaac (Gen 17:19) and Jacob (Exod 2:24). Jacob’s twelve sons were the ancestors of Israel’s twelve tribes. Israel’s liberation from Egypt and settlement in Canaan were based on God’s promises to their ancestors, not on the Israelites’ own virtues (Deut 9:4-5).

notes.zh: 神與亞伯拉罕（當時名叫亞伯蘭，創15:18）開始立約，又與以撒（創17:19）和雅各（出2:24）延續這約。雅各的十二個兒子是以色列十二支派的祖先。以色列脫離埃及、在迦南定居，是根據神對他們祖先的應許，而不是因為以色列人自己的美德（申9:4-5）。

notes.en: As a conclusion to the book, this chapter discusses various types of vows and ends with a provision for redeeming one’s tithes (see also ch 25). Under certain circumstances, such as an emergency, an individual might make a vow promising something to God, usually in exchange for God’s answering his or her prayer (see Jon 2:9). Once the prayer is answered, the individual might be tempted to discount the vow. Scripture requires that vows be made carefully (see Lev 5:4; Eccl 5:4-6) and then carried out. Jesus taught that oaths should not be commonly or carelessly made (Matt 5:33-37; 23:16-22).

notes.zh: 這一章作為全書的結尾，討論各種的許願，最後講到贖回十分之一的規定（又見第25章）。在某些情況下，例如遇到急難時，人可能會向神許願，答應獻上某樣東西，通常是為了求神應允他的禱告（見拿2:9）。禱告蒙應允之後，人可能會想打折扣。聖經要求人要謹慎許願（見利5:4；傳5:4-6），許了就要還。耶穌教導，人不可隨便或輕率地起誓（太5:33-37；23:16-22）。

notes.en: The vow taken to become a Nazirite is also called a special vow (Num 6:2), but the vow mentioned here was probably a promise made to God when seeking a desired answer to prayer (see Gen 28:20-22). Pagan religions of the time sacrificed infants to their gods, but God outlawed such a practice (Lev 18:21; 20:2-5; cp. Gen 22:12-13). Consequently, the concept of being vowed to the Lord was measured in terms of service given, not in the sacrifice of a life. Whether the vow was made by the person or by another acting for him or her, payment was to be made to the sanctuary, apparently for the person’s expenses during the term of service. See also Num 6:1-21; Judg 13:5, 7; 1 Sam 1:11; Amos 2:11-12; Acts 18:18.

notes.zh: 成為拿細耳人的願也稱為「特許的願」（民6:2），但這裡所說的願，大概是人為求禱告蒙應允而向神許的願（見創28:20-22）。當時的異教會把嬰孩獻給他們的神明，但神禁止這種做法（利18:21；20:2-5；參創22:12-13）。因此，「被許給耶和華」的觀念是以所獻上的事奉來衡量，而不是獻上一條生命。無論是本人許願，或由別人代他許願，都要付款給聖所，看來是為了支付這人在事奉期間的費用。又見民6:1-21；士13:5、7；撒上1:11；摩2:11-12；徒18:18。

notes.en: This section reflects social rank in ancient Near Eastern cultures. An adult man of working age had the highest rank, followed by an adult woman of working age. A boy ranked higher than a girl, and both ranked higher than toddlers. Senior citizens, who were past prime working age, ranked comparably to boys and girls. • The amount of fifty shekels (see study note on 5:15) would have represented about 20 ounces (570 grams) of silver, a significant amount. Comparisons with other literature of the time indicates that the biblical valuation is quite high and would have been out of reach for most people.

五十舍客勒（見5:15的注釋）大約是570公克的銀子，是一筆可觀的數目。和當時其他文獻比較，聖經所定的價值相當高，大多數人都付不起。

notes.en: As in the offering system (see 5:7-13), special consideration was given to the poor person who wanted to contribute to the sanctuary. In such cases, the amount of silver to accompany the pledge was left to the priest’s discretion.

notes.zh: 和獻祭制度一樣（見5:7-13），想要奉獻給聖所的窮人會得到特別的考量。在這種情況下，隨許願所付的銀子數目，由祭司斟酌決定。

notes.en: Once an acceptable animal had been vowed and the priest at the sanctuary had accepted it on God’s behalf, the animal became holy and belonged to God.

notes.zh: 合用的牲畜一旦許了願，聖所的祭司又代表神接受了，這牲畜就「成為聖」，屬於神。

notes.en: An unclean animal, one unfit either for food or sacrifice, could be bought back by the worshiper for its assessed value plus 20 percent. No doubt the reasoning behind this rule was to preserve the sanctity of vows and to minimize thoughtless dedications. For the 20 percent surcharge on property, see 27:15, 19, 31.

notes.en: The Hebrew term translated as dedicates is quite strong and means “declares holy.” • This ruling would apply only to a house in a walled town. Other houses, whether in unwalled villages or on open land, reverted to the owner in the Year of Jubilee (25:29-31). If the owner decided to redeem it, he had to pay a surcharge of 20 percent. If the house was not redeemed in the first year, it became the property of the sanctuary and priests, and it could be used however they wished.

譯作「分別為聖」的希伯來字語氣很強，意思是「宣告為聖」。

這條規定只適用於有城牆之城內的房屋。其他房屋，無論在無城牆的村莊或在曠野，到了禧年都要歸還原主（25:29-31）。屋主若決定贖回，要另付五分之一。房屋若在第一年內沒有贖回，就成為聖所和祭司的產業，他們可以隨意使用。

notes.en: The price for dedicating a field was determined by the number of years remaining until the next Year of Jubilee (see 25:24-28). If this property was not redeemed, it became the property of the priests to do with as they wished. The price of redeeming a field was 120 percent of the valuation (see 27:11-13). If a landowner dedicated his field without redeeming it, it did not revert to his family in the Year of Jubilee.

notes.zh: 分別為聖之田地的價值，按距離下一個禧年還有幾年來決定（見25:24-28）。這地業若沒有贖回，就成為祭司的產業，他們可以隨意處理。贖回田地的價錢是估定價值的一又五分之一倍（見27:11-13）。地主若把田地分別為聖而沒有贖回，到了禧年也不歸還他的家族。

notes.en: Year of Jubilee: See 25:8-55. • specially set apart: An acceptable vow devoting something to the Lord made it holy; it could not be redeemed.

notes.en: You may not dedicate: Every firstborn male, be it man or animal, already belonged to God (Exod 13:2; 34:19-20). Therefore, dedicating a firstborn was a useless exercise. The priest clearly had a use for the firstborn of animals fit for food or sacrifice (clean animals). The firstborn of a ceremonially unclean animal such as a donkey could be redeemed for 20 percent more than its value. Human firstborns had to be redeemed (Exod 13:11-13).

notes.en: specially set apart (Hebrew kherem): Such an act of devotion was irrevocable. The person, animal, or property devoted this way was dedicated to the service of the sanctuary in a manner defined by the priest.

notes.en: set apart for destruction (Hebrew kherem): The context here is the war for the conquest of Canaan, when cities, animals, and people deemed holy to some other god were set apart to be destroyed.

notes.en: One-tenth (the “tithe”) of the harvest belonged to the Lord (Deut 14:22-26; cp. Lev 23:10-14). Members of the tribe of Levi, the priests and Levites, received no tribal lands. Accordingly, they were allotted one tenth of all produce from those who did own land (Num 18:21-29). This tithe was set aside every year (Deut 14:22) and was taken to the sanctuary; part of it was eaten there in a ritual meal (Deut 14:23-26). A second tithe was paid locally every third year to the local Levites and the poor (Deut 14:27-29; 26:12; contrast Amos 4:4). The Levites then paid a tithe of what they received to the Tabernacle priests (Num 18:26), who used it to support themselves and maintain the sanctuary. Some interpreters think there were three tithes, the first paid to the Levites, the second consumed at the sanctuary, and the third paid every third year for the poor. Others suggest that there was just one tithe, paid at the sanctuary for two years, then paid locally every third year.

notes.zh: 收成的十分之一屬於耶和華（申14:22-26；參利23:10-14）。利未支派的祭司和利未人沒有分到支派的地業，所以他們從有地的人所有的出產中分得十分之一（民18:21-29）。這十分之一每年都要分出來（申14:22），帶到聖所，其中一部分在那裡的禮儀筵席中吃掉（申14:23-26）。每第三年又在本地繳納第二個十分之一，給當地的利未人和窮人（申14:27-29；26:12；對照摩4:4）。利未人再把所得的十分之一交給會幕的祭司（民18:26），供養祭司並維持聖所。有些解經家認為共有三種十分之一：第一種給利未人，第二種在聖所吃掉，第三種每三年一次給窮人。也有人認為只有一種十分之一，頭兩年在聖所繳納，第三年在本地繳納。

notes.en: The penalty to buy back the tithed harvest was the same amount assessed for an individual who had accidentally withheld his tithe (see 5:16).
